
`run_service.py` reuses the `inbound`, `status` and `post` helpers from the
step 4 test. The second delivery also shows up in the log, as a `WARNING`
from `BaseRepository` (`IntegrityError on ZapMessageModel.add: unique
violation; table=zap_messages; columns=message_id; ...`) — that is the claim
working, not an error.

Now each piece.

### What `ZapInbox` does for you

**`claim`: idempotency by `messageId`.** Deliveries go through the gateway's
`callback_deliveries` queue, with retries: the same message arrives more than
once when your answer is lost, or when the gateway restarts mid-`POST`. The
`UNIQUE` on `message_id` is the claim — the insert of whoever arrives second
hits it and `claim` returns `duplicate`. There is no `exists` before the
insert: two replicas checking at the same time would both see "not there"
and both store. A conflict whose `message_id` is **not** stored is not a
duplicate (another constraint on your table refused the row) and is raised.
See [Idempotency](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/idempotency.md) for the same reasoning on your own routes.

**`claim`: only a person's conversation.** `accepted_servers` defaults to
`ZapJidServerEnum.USER` and `ZapJidServerEnum.LID`; groups, broadcasts and channels
come back `skipped` without being stored. Pass another `frozenset` to accept
more.

**`claim`: media only through the gateway.** The gateway downloads the media
when the message arrives, and WhatsApp does not serve it again afterwards.
`claim` downloads nothing: it stores the `media_type`, and whoever needs the
bytes calls `client.get_message_media(message_id)`. When `media_type` is set
and `media_url` is `None`, the download failed or went over
`MEDIA_MAX_BYTES`: the row is stored and `claim` returns `media-lost`.

**`track`: status out of order, and before the send.** Each delivery has its
own retry and backoff, so a `sent` whose first `POST` failed can land after
the `delivered`. And the gateway guards its **own** row against regression,
but sends the callback anyway. `track` applies the status only when
`is_forward_transition(current, new)` says it moves forward:

- the ladder is `queued < sending < sent < delivered < read`;
- repeating the current status, or stepping down the ladder, is not forward;
- `failed` is terminal — nothing overwrites it —, and it only overwrites
  `queued`, `sending` and `sent`, because `delivered` and `read` already prove
  the message arrived; the callback's `error` goes to the `error` column.

The row is keyed by the callback's `id` — the outbox row the send's `202`
returned — and is **created** when it does not exist: the gateway can call
back before the send was committed, and answering `404` would only spend its
retries.

**`send_text`: one record per key.** The send stores the delivery row with
the `202`'s `id` and the `idempotency_key`. On a re-delivery, the same key
makes the gateway answer `deduped=True`, and `send_text` finds the row by the
key instead of creating another. If `track` already created the row from a
callback, `send_text` only attaches the key — and never steps the status
down. A `202` that is already `failed` raises `ZapSendFailedException`
(`502`, `code="ZAP_SEND_FAILED"`) and records nothing.

!!! note "The commit belongs to `BaseRepository`, not to the session"
    `db.session_dependency` does **not** commit at the end of the request.
    Every `ZapInbox` write goes through `BaseRepository.add` or `update`,
    which commit. Changing a row's attribute without calling `update` looks
    like it works in a test and stores nothing.

!!! tip "Why `text` is `Text` and nullable"
    A media message without a caption arrives without `text`, and a WhatsApp
    message has no 255-character ceiling. `ZapInboundMessageMixin` declares
    `text` as a nullable `Text`. A required `String(255)` column refuses the
    captionless media on any database, and the long text on PostgreSQL —
    SQLite ignores the declared length and stores it all, so an in-memory
    test does not show it.

### Your service: the reply

`ZapBotService.receive` calls `claim` and replies on both paths, `stored`
**and** `duplicate`. If it replied only on `stored`, a send that failed after
the insert would never be redone: the re-delivery would land on `duplicate`.
With `idempotency_key=f"reply-{message_id}"`, on the re-delivery the gateway
returns the original row with `deduped=True` instead of sending twice (the
second `gateway:` line of the output above).

**`chatKey`, not `from`.** `from_` is the raw address, and the same person
can arrive through a number and later through a LID — grouping by `from_`
splits one conversation in two. `chat_key` is the number's digits, already
resolved by the gateway from the LID; it is also the `to` that `send_text`
accepts. It is `None` for a LID the gateway could not map — `claim` stores
it, but there is no one to reply to.

### The controller: pick the path, nothing else

`ZapWebhookController.handle` looks at which body the delivery carries and
calls `receive` or `inbox.track`. It opens no session, decides no rule, knows
nothing about the gateway. If tomorrow the same event must trigger two things
(store and notify another service), this is where both calls meet.

### The dependencies and the router

`get_zap_bot_service` builds the `ZapInbox` over the request's session
(`db.session_dependency`) and over the `ZapClient` the `lifespan` opened and
kept in `app.state`; `get_zap_webhook_controller` builds the controller over
the service. The router receives both through `Depends` and keeps a single
line, `return await controller.handle(delivery)`.

!!! note "Why the `ZapClient` is born in the `lifespan`"
    A closed `HTTPClient` does not reopen. Created at module level, it
    survives a single `lifespan`: the suite's second `TestClient(app)` finds
    the client closed and fails with `RuntimeError: Cannot send a request, as
    the client has been closed`. Created inside the `lifespan`, every
    start-up of the application gets its own.

### Where each piece lives in your service

The single file is there so the example runs. In the Tempest service layout,
each class goes to its layer:

```text
src/
├── api/
│   ├── dependencies/
│   │   ├── controllers.py   # get_zap_webhook_controller
│   │   └── services.py      # get_zap_client, get_zap_bot_service
│   └── routers/
│       └── webhooks.py      # router + receive_zap
├── controllers/
│   └── zap_webhook.py       # ZapWebhookController
├── services/
│   └── zap_bot.py           # ZapBotService (over the SDK's ZapInbox)
├── schemas/
│   └── zap.py               # ZapWebhookResponseSchema
└── db/
    └── models/
        └── zap.py           # ZapMessageModel, ZapDeliveryModel
```

`verify_zap` sits next to the other authentication dependencies
(`api/dependencies/auth.py`), reading the secret from settings.

## Step 4 — Testing without the gateway

Sign the body the way the gateway does and send it through the `TestClient`.
The fixture opens the `TestClient` as a context manager so the `lifespan`
runs — without it neither `create_tables` nor the `ZapClient` run, and the
first delivery fails with
`AttributeError: 'State' object has no attribute 'zap'`.

```python title="test_zap_service.py"
import hashlib
import hmac
import json
from collections.abc import Iterator
from typing import Any

import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from zap_service import app

SECRET: str = "my-secret"
WHEN: str = "2026-04-21T18:30:00.000Z"


def inbound(message_id: str, sender: str, **fields: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Build a ``message.received`` body the way the gateway sends it.

    Args:
        message_id (str): The ``messageId``.
        sender (str): The raw JID in ``from``.
        **fields (Any): Extra fields (``text``, ``chatKey``, ``mediaType``…).

    Returns:
        dict[str, Any]: The body, ready to sign.
    """
    return {
        "event": "message.received",
        "messageId": message_id,
        "from": sender,
        "timestamp": WHEN,
        **fields,
    }


def status(outbound_id: str, value: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Build a status callback body the way the gateway sends it.

    Args:
        outbound_id (str): The ``id`` the send's ``202`` answered.
        value (str): ``sent``, ``delivered``, ``read`` or ``failed``.

    Returns:
        dict[str, Any]: The body, ready to sign.
    """
    return {
        "event": f"message.{value}",
        "id": outbound_id,
        "consumer": "bot",
        "to": "5511999999999",
        "kind": "text",
        "status": value,
        "timestamp": WHEN,
    }


def post(client: TestClient, payload: dict[str, Any], secret: str = SECRET) -> Any:
    """Sign and deliver a body, like the gateway's callback worker.

    Args:
        client (TestClient): The application's client.
        payload (dict[str, Any]): The body.
        secret (str): The secret to sign with.

    Returns:
        Any: The route's response.
    """
    body: bytes = json.dumps(payload).encode()
    digest: str = hmac.new(secret.encode(), body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return client.post(
        "/webhooks/zap",
        content=body,
        headers={"x-zap-signature": f"sha256={digest}"},
    )


@pytest.fixture
def client() -> Iterator[TestClient]:
    """Start the application with its lifespan (tables + gateway client).

    Yields:
        TestClient: The application's client.
    """
    with TestClient(app) as test_client:
        yield test_client


def test_wrong_secret_is_401(client: TestClient) -> None:
    """A delivery signed with another secret is refused."""
    response = post(client, inbound("A1", "5511999999999@s.whatsapp.net"), "outro")
    assert response.status_code == 401


def test_message_is_stored_once(client: TestClient) -> None:
    """The gateway's redelivery becomes ``duplicate``, not a second row."""
    payload = inbound(
        "A2", "5511999999999@s.whatsapp.net", chatKey="5511999999999", text="Hi"
    )
    assert post(client, payload).json() == {"outcome": "stored"}
    assert post(client, payload).json() == {"outcome": "duplicate"}


def test_group_is_skipped(client: TestClient) -> None:
    """A group message is neither stored nor answered."""
    payload = inbound("A3", "120363000000000000@g.us", text="good morning")
    assert post(client, payload).json() == {"outcome": "skipped"}


def test_lost_media(client: TestClient) -> None:
    """``mediaType`` without ``mediaUrl`` is lost media."""
    payload = inbound("A4", "5511999999999@s.whatsapp.net", mediaType="audio")
    assert post(client, payload).json() == {"outcome": "media-lost"}


def test_late_status_is_stale(client: TestClient) -> None:
    """A ``delivered`` after the ``read`` does not move the status back."""
    assert post(client, status("out-9", "read")).json() == {"outcome": "applied"}
    assert post(client, status("out-9", "delivered")).json() == {"outcome": "stale"}


def test_unknown_event_is_200(client: TestClient) -> None:
    """An event the SDK does not model answers ``200``, so it is not retried."""
    payload = {"event": "message.edited", "messageId": "A2"}
    assert post(client, payload).json() == {"outcome": "ignored"}
```

```console
$ pytest test_zap_service.py -v
test_zap_service.py::test_wrong_secret_is_401 PASSED
test_zap_service.py::test_message_is_stored_once PASSED
test_zap_service.py::test_group_is_skipped PASSED
test_zap_service.py::test_lost_media PASSED
test_zap_service.py::test_late_status_is_stale PASSED
test_zap_service.py::test_unknown_event_is_200 PASSED
============================== 6 passed in 0.68s ===============================
```

!!! check "Signature cross-checked with the gateway"
    The standard library's `hmac` produces the same header as the gateway's
    `signPayload` (`src/utils/signature.ts`): the SDK's suite pins two
    signatures produced by the gateway **itself** and checks that they pass
    (`tests/integrations/messaging/zap/test_webhooks.py`).

## Recap

- Register the webhook **with** `--secret`; without it the gateway does not
  sign.
- `make_zap_webhook_dependency(secret=...)` verifies the HMAC over the raw
  body and returns a `ZapWebhookDelivery`.
- Dispatch on `delivery.inbound` / `delivery.status`; whatever has neither
  answers `200` and goes to the log.
- Compare against the enums — `ZapWebhookEventEnum`, `ZapInboundMediaTypeEnum`,
  `ZapJidServerEnum`, `ZapOutboundKindEnum`, `AcceptedResponseStatus` — not loose
  strings; `is` on the envelope and on `from_server`, `==` on body fields.
- Filter on `from_server`: groups, status stories and channels arrive too.
- `ZapInbox` + `ZapInboundMessageMixin` / `ZapDeliveryMixin` bring
  idempotency through `UNIQUE` on `message_id` (inbound) and `outbound_id`
  (status and send); the reply to the sender uses an `idempotency_key`
  derived from `message_id`.
- Group and reply by `chat_key`; `None` is a group or a LID with no number.
- Media only through `get_message_media`, and `media_url: None` with
  `media_type` means lost.
- `ZapInbox.track` applies `is_forward_transition` before writing any
  status, and creates the row of a callback that arrives before the send.
- Router → controller → service → repository: the route keeps one line, and
  the rules are testable without HTTP.

Source: https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/refresh-tokens.md

# DB-backed refresh tokens (rotation + revocation)

Since **v0.66.0** the bundled auth flow can swap the *stateless* JWT refresh token for an **opaque token persisted in the database**, gaining three things a plain JWT never gives you: **real rotation**, **reuse detection** (stolen token), and **revocation** (logout that kills the session before its expiry).

It is all **opt-in**: you pass a `refresh_token_model` to the service. Without it, the SDK keeps the stateless behavior it always had — zero breaking change.

!!! info "Installation"
    The refresh-token models (`BaseUserRefreshTokenModel`) ship with `tempest-fastapi-sdk`. `UserAuthService` and `make_auth_router` need the `[auth]` extra — `uv add "tempest-fastapi-sdk[auth]"` (pulls in `bcrypt` + `PyJWT`).

## What's in this recipe

1. **[Stateless vs DB-backed in 30 seconds](#stateless-vs-db-backed)** — what changes and why.
2. **[Setup](#setup)** — the `BaseUserRefreshTokenModel` table.
3. **[Wiring](#wiring)** — pass `refresh_token_model` to the service + router.
4. **[How rotation works](#rotation)** — families, single-use, reuse.
5. **[Logout](#logout)** — the `POST /auth/logout` endpoint.
6. **[Using only `UserAuthService`](#service-direct)** — without the router.
7. **[Security](#security)**.
8. **[Next steps](#next-steps)**.

---

## Stateless vs DB-backed

A **stateless refresh token** is just a JWT signed with the `refresh` claim. The server trusts it if the signature matches and it has not expired — **there is no database row**. Simple, but:

- You cannot **revoke** it (logout kills nothing — the token lives until `exp`).
- There is no **real rotation**: you mint a new pair, but the old one stays valid in parallel.
- There is no **reuse detection**: a stolen token works for days and nobody notices.

A **DB-backed refresh token** is an **opaque** value (random, no claims) whose SHA-256 hash lives in a table. Every `POST /auth/refresh`:

1. Marks the presented token `used_at` (single-use).
2. Mints a new token in the **same family** (the rotation lineage of that login).
3. If anyone replays an **already-rotated** token, that is the classic stolen-token signal → **the whole family is revoked**.

!!! info "Why opaque and not JWT-with-jti?"
    An opaque token forces the database to be the single source of truth. There are no claims to decode, no window between "signature valid" and "row revoked". The access token **stays** a stateless JWT (short, no per-request lookup) — only the refresh becomes DB-backed.

---

## Setup

The table is abstract in the SDK (`BaseUserRefreshTokenModel`) — your application ships the concrete table, just like `BaseUserTokenModel` / `BaseUserRecoveryCodeModel`. Use the `make_user_refresh_token_model` helper to bind the FK to your users table:

```python
# src/db/models/__init__.py
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    make_user_refresh_token_model,
    make_user_token_model,
)

from src.db.models.user import UserModel

UserRefreshTokenModel = make_user_refresh_token_model(
    user_table="users",
    tablename="user_refresh_tokens",
    class_name="UserRefreshTokenModel",
)
```

Or, if you prefer a hand-written class (recommended in production, for refactors and stable imports):

```python
# src/db/models/user_refresh_token.py
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from uuid import UUID

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import BaseUserRefreshTokenModel


class UserRefreshTokenModel(BaseUserRefreshTokenModel):
    """Concrete opaque refresh-token table."""

    __tablename__ = "user_refresh_tokens"

    user_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        ForeignKey("users.id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        nullable=False,
        index=True,
    )
```

The table carries: `token_hash` (unique, indexed), `family_id` (rotation lineage), `expires_at`, `used_at` (rotated), and `revoked_at` (logout / family kill).

!!! info "The `tempest` command needs the `[cli]` extra (or `[cli-ops]` on a server)"
    Without either, `tempest` exits with code 2 and prints how to install it.
    In development: `uv add --dev "tempest-fastapi-sdk[cli]"`. Details in
    [Installation → CLI](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/installation.md#cli).

!!! warning "Migration required"
    It is a new table. Run `uv run tempest db revision -m "refresh tokens"` + `uv run tempest db upgrade` before shipping.

---

## Wiring

Pass the concrete model to `UserAuthService`. **That alone** turns on DB-backed mode — the router detects it and mounts `/auth/logout` on its own:

```python
# src/api/dependencies/services.py

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import UserAuthService

from src.core.settings import settings
from src.db.models import UserModel, UserRefreshTokenModel, UserTokenModel


def get_auth_service() -> UserAuthService:
    """Build the bundled auth service in DB-backed refresh mode."""
    return UserAuthService(
        user_model=UserModel,
        token_model=UserTokenModel,
        auth_settings=settings,
        jwt_settings=settings,
        refresh_token_model=UserRefreshTokenModel,  # <- turns on DB-backed mode
    )
```

The refresh-token TTL reuses `JWT_REFRESH_TTL_SECONDS` (default 7 days) — no new setting.

!!! check "Migrating from stateless"
    Adopting DB-backed mode does not invalidate existing sessions up front, but old JWT refresh tokens **stop being accepted** (`/refresh` now looks them up in the database). Force a fresh login after the deploy, or run a grace period accepting both in your own handler.

---

## Rotation

Every login (or auto-activated signup / activation / reset / mfa-verify) creates a token in a **fresh family**. Every refresh rotates within the same family:

```text
login ──> tokenA (family F)
  │
  └─ POST /refresh (tokenA) ──> tokenA.used_at set, mint tokenB (family F)
        │
        └─ POST /refresh (tokenB) ──> tokenB.used_at set, mint tokenC (family F)
```

If an attacker steals `tokenA` and tries to use it **after** you have already rotated to `tokenB`:

```text
POST /refresh (tokenA)  # tokenA.used_at != null  ->  REUSE DETECTED
  └─ revoke the WHOLE family F (tokenA, tokenB, tokenC...)
  └─ 401
```

Result: both the attacker and the victim are logged out on their next attempt. The victim logs in again (a small annoyance), the attacker loses access (a big win).

!!! danger "Single-use is mandatory for reuse detection to work"
    The client **must** discard the old refresh token after each `/refresh` and keep the new one. Reusing a rotated token triggers the family kill — that is not a bug, it is the feature.

!!! info "Two redemptions at once"
    The database decides the rotation in a conditional
    `UPDATE ... WHERE used_at IS NULL`: two concurrent `POST /refresh` with
    the same token yield **one** new pair and **one** 401, and the 401
    revokes the family — including the child the other one just received.
    Before, both read the token as free and each got a live child, with no
    reuse detected.

!!! info "The revocation is committed, and the request rolled back first (v0.252.0)"
    The family kill has to survive the 401 that immediately follows it. In a FastAPI request the exception leaves through the session dependency's teardown, so up to v0.251.0 the revocation — which only went through `flush()` — went away with the rollback: the replay was refused and **every descendant kept working**.

    Now, on reuse detection, the service rolls the request's session back, applies the family `UPDATE`, and **commits**. Two consequences for your handler:

    - Any write the request had staged before `/refresh` is dropped. It would have been dropped anyway — the request is closing with a 401 — and committing it as a side effect of a security decision would be a surprise.
    - Objects loaded in that session before the error are expired. If your `except` reads an attribute off an earlier object, reload it.

---

## Logout

With DB-backed mode on, the router mounts `POST /auth/logout`:

```python
import httpx


async def logout(refresh_token: str) -> None:
    """Revoke a session via the bundled logout endpoint."""
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="http://localhost:8000") as client:
        response = await client.post(
            "/auth/logout",
            json={"refresh_token": refresh_token, "all_sessions": False},
        )
        response.raise_for_status()  # 204 No Content
```

- `all_sessions=False` (default) — revoke only the token's **family** (that login).
- `all_sessions=True` — revoke **all** of the user's refresh tokens (log out everywhere).

The endpoint is **idempotent**: an unknown or already-revoked token still returns `204` and never leaks whether the token existed.

!!! note "Absent in stateless mode"
    Without `refresh_token_model` the `/auth/logout` route is **not mounted** — a stateless JWT cannot be revoked, so the endpoint would make no sense.

---

## Service direct

Those who build their own endpoints use the service without the router. The three methods:

```python
from uuid import UUID

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import UserAuthService

from src.db.models import UserModel


async def issue(
    service: UserAuthService, session: AsyncSession, user: UserModel
) -> None:
    """Emit a DB-backed pair, rotate it, then revoke the session."""
    access, refresh = await service.issue_token_pair(session, user)
    await session.commit()

    # Rotate: mark the old token used, mint a new one in the same family.
    _user, new_access, new_refresh = await service.refresh_tokens(
        session, refresh_token=refresh
    )
    await session.commit()

    # Logout: revoke the family (or all_sessions=True for everything).
    await service.revoke_refresh_token(session, refresh_token=new_refresh)
    await session.commit()
```

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `issue_token_pair(session, user, *, family_id=None)` | Emit `(access, refresh)`. Opaque+persisted when a model is wired; stateless JWT otherwise. |
| `refresh_tokens(session, *, refresh_token)` | Rotate. Detects reuse → revokes the family. Returns `(user, access, refresh)`. |
| `revoke_refresh_token(session, *, refresh_token, all_sessions=False)` | Logout. Revokes the family (or everything). Idempotent. |

!!! tip "issue_jwt_pair still exists"
    The synchronous `issue_jwt_pair(user)` (pure stateless) stays available for back-compat. In DB-backed mode prefer `issue_token_pair`, which takes the `session` and persists the row.

---

## Security

- **Only the hash in the database.** The refresh token plaintext is returned **once** at issuance; the database stores only the SHA-256. A database leak yields no usable tokens.
- **Single-use + family.** Mandatory rotation + family kill turn a refresh-token theft from "access for days" into "one attempt and both go down".
- **Access token unchanged.** Still a short stateless JWT (`JWT_ACCESS_TTL_SECONDS`, default 1h) — no per-request lookup. DB-backed is for the refresh only.
- **CASCADE.** The FK with `ondelete="CASCADE"` wipes the tokens alongside the user.

!!! warning "Change the `JWT_SECRET`"
    The access token is still signed with `JWT_SECRET`. The default `"change-me-change-me-change-me-32"` is a placeholder — override it in production, otherwise the access token is forgeable (and then the DB-backed refresh does not save you).

---

## Recap

- A stateless refresh token is a JWT the server accepts because the signature
  checks out; it cannot be revoked before it expires. The DB-backed mode trades
  that for a persisted opaque token.
- The table is abstract (`BaseUserRefreshTokenModel`); your service ships the
  concrete one, as it already does for the account token.
- Passing the concrete model to `UserAuthService` is the **only** step that
  turns the mode on: the router detects it and mounts `/auth/logout` itself.
- Every login opens a **family**; every refresh rotates inside it. Reusing an
  already-rotated token is a theft signal, and it revokes the whole family.
- Only the hash reaches the database. The plaintext is returned once, at
  issue time.
- If you mount your own endpoints, three service methods cover it without the
  router.

## Next steps

- **[Auth flow (signup/reset)](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/auth-flow.md)** — the full flow where tokens are issued.
- **[MFA (TOTP / 2FA)](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/mfa.md)** — second factor; `mfa-verify` also emits the DB-backed pair.
- **[Security](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/security.md)** — rate limit, idempotency, CSRF middlewares.

### Recap

- `refresh_token_model=` turns on DB-backed mode — without it, stateless as always.
- Refresh becomes **opaque** (hash in the database); access stays a JWT.
- **Single-use** rotation + **family** = reuse detection → `POST /auth/refresh` kills the family on a theft.
- `POST /auth/logout` revokes a session (or all with `all_sessions=true`); mounted only in DB-backed mode.

# Resumable uploads (tus)

A field technician takes ten photos with no signal; when the network comes back they go
up — and if the connection drops halfway through the third one, the upload continues
from the byte where it stopped, not from zero. In the browser that is
`tempest-react-sdk`'s `createResumableUpload`, which speaks the
[tus 1.0.0](https://tus.io/protocols/resumable-upload) protocol. This recipe builds the
server side with `make_tus_router`.

!!! info "No new extra"
    The router and `LocalTusStore` use only what the base install already ships
    (FastAPI and the stdlib). `S3TusStore` over `AsyncMinIOClient` needs the `[minio]`
    extra.

## The minimal example

```python
from pathlib import Path
from uuid import UUID

from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    LocalTusStore,
    TusStore,
    TusUpload,
    make_tus_router,
    register_exception_handlers,
)


async def current_user_id() -> UUID:
    return UUID("00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001")


async def photo_received(upload: TusUpload, store: TusStore, /) -> None:
    print("upload complete:", upload.id, upload.filename, upload.length)


store = LocalTusStore(Path("var/tus"))
app = FastAPI()
register_exception_handlers(app)
app.include_router(
    make_tus_router(
        store,
        current_user_id=current_user_id,
        on_complete=photo_received,
    ),
)
```

Replace `current_user_id` above with the authentication dependency your service already
uses (the one that returns the signed-in user's id). On the frontend:

```ts
const done = await createResumableUpload({
  endpoint: "/api/uploads",
  file,
  metadata: { filename: file.name },
  getToken: auth.getToken,
}).start();
```

The default `prefix` is `/api/uploads`, the same `endpoint` as the `tempest-react-sdk`
examples.

## What the client sends — and what the router answers

The implemented subset is exactly what `createResumableUpload` sends. Measured two ways:
reading `src/http/resumable-upload.ts` and its tests, and running the real client
(bundled from source with `esbuild`, on Node 24, over the `fetch` transport) against this
router: a 1 MiB file in 256 KiB chunks, paused halfway, resumed by a second handle — as
after a reload — with the `sha256` of the file on disk equal to the client's.

| Step | Client request | Router response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create | `POST /api/uploads` + `Tus-Resumable`, `Upload-Length`, `Idempotency-Key`, `Upload-Metadata` (when there is metadata) | `201` + relative `Location` (`/api/uploads/<id>`) + `Upload-Expires` |
| Probe | `HEAD /api/uploads/<id>` + `Tus-Resumable` | `200` + `Upload-Offset`, `Upload-Length`, `Cache-Control: no-store` |
| Write | `PATCH /api/uploads/<id>` + `Tus-Resumable`, `Upload-Offset`, `Content-Type: application/offset+octet-stream`, body = chunk | `204` + the new `Upload-Offset` |
| Discard | `DELETE /api/uploads/<id>` + `Tus-Resumable` (on `abort({ discard: true })`) | `204` |

Plus what the client adds depending on its options: `Authorization: Bearer` (with
`getToken`), `X-CSRF-Token` on `POST`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` — never on `HEAD` — (with
`csrf`), and the static `headers`. The router reads none of them: authentication is your
`current_user_id` dependency, and CSRF is the app's `CSRFMiddleware`.

Left out because the client never sends them: `OPTIONS` discovery,
`Upload-Defer-Length`, a body on the `POST` (*creation-with-upload*), *checksum*,
*concatenation* and `X-HTTP-Method-Override`.

??? note "Why `Location` is relative"
    The client resolves `Location` against the URL the `POST` went to (RFC 9110). A
    relative path needs no knowledge of the host and scheme the proxy exposes; behind a
    `root_path` (`/svc`), `Location` comes out as `/svc/api/uploads/<id>` — covered in
    `tests/storage/tus/test_router.py`.

## The finished file: `on_complete`

When the last byte arrives, the router calls `on_complete(upload, store)` **once per
upload, inside the request of the last `PATCH`**, under the upload's lock, before the
`204`. That is where the service registers the photo or moves the file:

```python
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LocalTusStore, TusStore, TusUpload

ARCHIVE = Path("var/photos")


async def archive_photo(upload: TusUpload, store: TusStore, /) -> None:
    assert isinstance(store, LocalTusStore)
    name = upload.filename or "photo.bin"
    shutil.move(store.data_path(upload.id), ARCHIVE / f"{upload.id}-{name}")
    await store.delete(upload.id)
```

- `upload.metadata` holds the decoded `Upload-Metadata` (base64 → UTF-8), as the client
  sent it — `nota-ação.webm` arrives with its accent.
- `upload.filename` is the **sanitized** name: only the last path component, letters,
  digits and `-_. ()`. `../../etc/passwd` becomes `passwd`. Use it, never
  `metadata["filename"]`, to build a path.
- `store.stream(upload.id)` reads the bytes from any store; `LocalTusStore.data_path` and
  `S3TusStore.object_key` give the path and the key, to move without copying through the
  process.
- `await store.delete(upload.id)` inside the callback is allowed: the router does not
  recreate the record, and the next `HEAD` answers `404`. The example above runs in
  `tests/storage/tus/test_hardening.py`, read straight from this page.
- A `PATCH` to an upload that is already complete — the empty one too, with
  `Upload-Offset` equal to the length — answers `409 TUS_UPLOAD_COMPLETED` without
  writing anything or calling the callback again. `createResumableUpload` handles every
  `409` by re-reading the offset with `HEAD` before the next attempt
  (`RESYNCABLE_STATUSES` in `resumable-upload.ts`, read in the code), and with the offset
  equal to the length the upload finishes.

!!! warning "A callback that raises"
    The `PATCH` answers `500`, and the upload stays complete with `notified = False`. The
    client does not retry: the next `HEAD` already shows every byte, so for it the upload
    is done. Find those uploads with
    `[u for u in await store.list_uploads() if u.completed and not u.notified]` and
    reprocess them — covered in `test_failing_on_complete_leaves_the_upload_complete_and_unnotified`.

## Upload owner

The `str()` of what `current_user_id` resolves becomes the owner, and the dependency must
return the user's **id** as `str`, `int` or `UUID`: any other type (the user model, a
claims dict) raises `TypeError` — the `str()` of an object can change between requests or
collide between users. Only the same value can
probe, continue or delete that upload; anyone else gets `404 TUS_UPLOAD_NOT_FOUND` — the
same `404` as an id that does not exist, so it never confirms the id is real.

Without `current_user_id`, the upload is anonymous and the URL is the only credential.
The id carries 192 random bits (`secrets.token_urlsafe(24)`, 32 characters), and the store
treats any id outside `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,128}` as absent: there is no `/`, `.` or `\`, so a
`LocalTusStore` path never leaves its directory.

## `Idempotency-Key` on creation

The client generates one key per upload and repeats it when the `201` is lost. The router
keeps `sha256(owner + key) → id` in the store itself:

- same key, same owner, same `Upload-Length` → the **same** `Location`;
- same key from another owner → another upload (the key never hands out someone else's URL);
- same key, same owner, another `Upload-Length` → `422 TUS_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`.

The mapping lives in the store (a file on disk, an object in the bucket), so it holds
after a restart.

Without `current_user_id` (anonymous mode) the key is **ignored**: with no owner, every
anonymous caller would share one key space, and whoever repeated someone else's key would
get their URL. The client generates the key with `crypto.randomUUID()` and, where the
browser does not offer it (outside a secure context, that is, without HTTPS), falls back
to a UUID built with `Math.random()`, which is not cryptographic randomness
(`src/http/idempotency.ts` in `tempest-react-sdk`). In anonymous mode, a creation retried
after a lost `201` leaves an orphan upload, which `purge_expired()` deletes. This route does not need `IdempotencyMiddleware`: that one keys the
cached response on a digest of the credentials, and a token refreshed between the attempt
and the retry no longer matches.

## MinIO / S3: `S3TusStore`

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AsyncMinIOClient, S3TusStore, make_tus_router

client = AsyncMinIOClient(
    endpoint="localhost:9000",
    access_key="minioadmin",
    secret_key="minioadmin",
    default_bucket="uploads",
)
router = make_tus_router(S3TusStore(client, prefix="tus/"))
```

S3 has no *append*, and a multipart part must be at least 5 MiB (except the last) — but
the client picks the chunk size, and `tempest-react-sdk`'s "Offline field app" recipe
sends 256 KiB. So each accepted `PATCH` becomes one small object, keyed by the offset it
starts at, and the file is assembled once, when the last byte arrives:

| Key | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `tus/<id>/info.json` | the record (offset, length, owner, expiry) |
| `tus/<id>/chunks/<20-digit offset>` | one object per `PATCH` |
| `tus/<id>/data` | the finished file, written at the end; the chunks are deleted |
| `tus/_idempotency/<digest>` | the id an `Idempotency-Key` created |

Everything lives in the bucket: another process, or another replica, sees the same
uploads.

The complete record is saved **before** the chunks are deleted. If the assembly fails
half-way, the `PATCH` answers `500`, the record stays at the previous offset and the
retried last chunk assembles again; if only deleting the chunks fails, the upload is
already complete and the leftover chunks go with `store.delete(id)` — both cases with an
injected failure in `test_hardening.py`.

`S3TusStore(min_chunk_size=...)` (64 KiB by default) refuses a chunk below it with
`400 TUS_CHUNK_TOO_SMALL`, except the one that ends the upload: every chunk is an object,
and without a floor a client sending 1 byte per `PATCH` would create one object per byte.
At 64 KiB a 1 GiB upload has at most 16 384 chunks; the client sends 5 MiB by default and
256 KiB in the field recipe.

!!! warning "The cost"
    Every byte is written to the bucket **twice** (chunk, then file) and read once. And
    the request of the last `PATCH` waits for the assembly, which spools the file through
    a temporary file on the server's disk (`SpooledTemporaryFile`, 8 MiB in memory before
    it goes to disk). For photos and recordings of a few MiB that is invisible; for
    multi-gigabyte files the last `PATCH` takes the time to read and rewrite the whole
    file — raise the proxy timeout, or prefer `LocalTusStore` on a shared disk. The
    temporary disk adds up per concurrent assembly: ten 1 GiB uploads finishing at once
    take up to 10 GiB in the server's temporary directory.

Measured against a real S3 server (SeaweedFS's S3 gateway in a container — the
`minio/minio` image answered *pull access denied* on this machine on 2026-11-22): 6 MiB
in 256 KiB chunks, the server killed with `SIGKILL` halfway, a new process resumes from
the offset stored in the bucket, and the final `data` object is byte-for-byte the upload,
with only `data` and `info.json` left (`tests/storage/tus/test_s3_live.py`,
`make test-docker`).

## Expiry and cleanup

An incomplete upload expires `expiration` after creation or after its last `PATCH` that
stored bytes (24 h by default) — an empty `PATCH` does not renew it; the deadline goes out as `Upload-Expires`. Past it, `HEAD` and
`PATCH` answer `410 TUS_UPLOAD_EXPIRED`, and the client starts over. A **complete**
upload never expires: its bytes already belong to the service.

Deleting what expired is up to you, on a schedule:

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LocalTusStore

store = LocalTusStore("var/tus")


async def sweep_uploads() -> list[str]:
    return await store.purge_expired()
```

`purge_expired()` returns the deleted ids (`[]` when nothing expired). Each upload is
re-read under the same per-upload lock the router uses, and one with a request in
progress is skipped. Hook it to a `TaskQueue` periodic task or a cron.

## Per-owner limits

Without a limit, a signed-in user creates uploads until the disk or the bucket is full.
Two router parameters close that, counting the owner's **unfinished, unexpired** uploads:

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LocalTusStore, make_tus_router

router = make_tus_router(
    LocalTusStore("var/tus"),
    max_uploads_per_owner=20,
    max_bytes_per_owner=2 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024,
)
```

Past either, the creation answers `403 TUS_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` with `details.limit`
(`"uploads"` or `"bytes"`) and `details.max`. Both default to `None`. They apply only with
`current_user_id`: in anonymous mode every caller would share one quota and one of them
would exhaust it for everyone, so none is enforced. An empty upload, which completes on
creation, never counts.

!!! warning "Cost of the check"
    Every creation with a limit reads every record in the store (`list_uploads()`). Keep
    the store swept with `purge_expired()`; with tens of thousands of live uploads this
    weighs on every `POST`.

## Concurrency and replicas

A `PATCH` takes the upload's lock **before** reading its body. A second `PATCH` (or
`DELETE`) to the same upload while the first is in progress answers
`409 TUS_UPLOAD_LOCKED` at once, without reading the body — through the same `409`
handling, the client re-reads with `HEAD` and retries after its backoff — so an upload never has two bodies spooled.
Measured with the interleaving forced (the first request held inside the write): 1 write,
the second at `409` with its body never read, the file holding only the first's bytes.
Without the lock, the same test shows both answering `204` for the same range
(`tests/storage/tus/test_concurrency.py`). The body goes to a `SpooledTemporaryFile` with
1 MiB in memory; the rest, up to `max_chunk_size`, goes to the temporary disk.

### Mobile networks: a body that stops half-way

A phone that loses signal mid-chunk leaves a half-open connection, with no FIN: the server
waits for the rest of the body until TCP gives up, minutes later — and since the lock is
taken before the body is read, every retry would answer `409 TUS_UPLOAD_LOCKED` until
then. So each piece of the body has a deadline: `body_read_timeout` (30 s by default).
When nothing arrives within it, the `PATCH` answers `408 TUS_BODY_READ_TIMEOUT`, **the
whole chunk is discarded** (the stored offset does not move; what arrived before the
deadline is not kept) and the lock is released. `408` is in the list of statuses
`createResumableUpload` retries (`RETRIABLE_STATUSES` in `errors.ts`), re-reading the
offset with `HEAD` first. An explicit disconnect mid-body stores nothing either: it becomes
an `INFO` log, not a `500`. Both cases run in `tests/storage/tus/test_resilience.py`, with
the app called as raw ASGI.

!!! warning "The lock is per process"
    Two replicas behind a load balancer can still race on one upload. With more than one
    replica, route an upload's requests to the same replica (sticky sessions on the
    `/api/uploads/<id>` path).

A restart, on the other hand, loses nothing: the record is written only after the bytes,
and it is the authority on the offset. Measured in `tests/storage/tus/test_restart.py`:
uvicorn in a subprocess, killed with `SIGKILL` after 192 KiB of 300 KiB; the new process,
built from nothing but the same directory, answers `HEAD` with `Upload-Offset: 196608`
and accepts the rest, and the final file is identical to the upload.

## CORS

A frontend on another origin can only read `Location` and `Upload-Offset` if the backend
exposes them — otherwise `getResponseHeader("Location")` returns `null` and the client
cannot find the upload it created:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from starlette.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import TUS_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS, TUS_CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://app.example.com"],
    allow_methods=["POST", "HEAD", "PATCH", "DELETE"],
    allow_headers=list(TUS_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS),
    expose_headers=list(TUS_CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS),
)
```

## Errors

Errors use the SDK envelope (`detail`/`code`/`details`). Every response of the tus routes
carries `Tus-Resumable: 1.0.0`, refusals included — the router's and a `401`/`403` raised
by your `current_user_id` dependency. The exception is an unhandled `500`: the app's
handler answers it, outside the route, without the header.

| Status | `code` | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `400` | `TUS_HEADER_INVALID` | `Upload-Length` or `Upload-Offset` missing, not a number or longer than 20 digits; `Upload-Metadata` not base64/UTF-8. `details.header` names the header |
| `400` | `TUS_CHUNK_TOO_SMALL` | a chunk that does not end the upload is below the store's `min_chunk_size`; `details.min_bytes` |
| `403` | `TUS_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` | the creation would pass `max_uploads_per_owner` or `max_bytes_per_owner` |
| `404` | `TUS_UPLOAD_NOT_FOUND` | unknown, malformed or someone else's id |
| `408` | `TUS_BODY_READ_TIMEOUT` | the `PATCH` body went longer than `body_read_timeout` without arriving; nothing is stored |
| `409` | `TUS_OFFSET_MISMATCH` | `Upload-Offset` differs from the stored one; `details.offset` is the server's |
| `409` | `TUS_UPLOAD_COMPLETED` | `PATCH` to an upload that already has every byte; nothing is stored |
| `409` | `TUS_UPLOAD_LOCKED` | another `PATCH`/`DELETE` of the same upload is in progress |
| `410` | `TUS_UPLOAD_EXPIRED` | incomplete upload past `Upload-Expires` |
| `412` | `TUS_VERSION_UNSUPPORTED` | `Tus-Resumable` missing or not `1.0.0`; the response carries `Tus-Version` |
| `413` | `TUS_UPLOAD_TOO_LARGE` | `Upload-Length` above `max_size` (with `Tus-Max-Size`), or a `PATCH` body past `Upload-Length` or `max_chunk_size`; nothing is stored |
| `415` | `TUS_CONTENT_TYPE_INVALID` | `PATCH` without `Content-Type: application/offset+octet-stream` |
| `422` | `TUS_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` | the key already created an upload of another size |

## Recap

- `make_tus_router(store, current_user_id=..., on_complete=...)` serves
  `createResumableUpload`: `POST`, `HEAD`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`.
- `LocalTusStore` keeps uploads on disk; `S3TusStore` in the bucket, one object per chunk
  and the assembly at the end (twice the writes, in exchange for accepting any chunk size).
- State survives a restart; the concurrency lock is per process.
- `on_complete` runs once per upload; a `PATCH` to a complete upload is `409`.
- `Idempotency-Key` per owner (ignored without one), per-owner limits, expiry with
  `purge_expired()`, a sanitized file name in `upload.filename`.


---

Source: https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/revenuecat.md

# RevenueCat (in-app subscriptions)

A Flutter (or native) app that sells subscriptions through the App Store and
Google Play almost always goes through RevenueCat. The app buys; RevenueCat
tells your backend through a **webhook** on every change (purchase, renewal,
cancellation, expiration...). The backend needs three things every service
ended up writing by hand:

1. **Authenticate** the webhook — and refuse everything when no secret is
   configured.
2. **Record the event exactly once**, answer `200` fast and process later —
   RevenueCat retries, and sometimes sends the same event twice.
3. **Give up on a poisoned event** after N attempts, instead of retrying it on
   every sweep, forever.

The SDK ships all three: the adapter in
`tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.subscriptions.revenuecat` and the generic
`WebhookInbox` in `tempest_fastapi_sdk.db`, which works for any provider.

!!! info "Installation"
    No extra. The client uses the SDK's `HTTPClient`, and `httpx` already
    ships with the base package.

!!! note "Where every claim about RevenueCat comes from"
    Event format, headers, event types and retry policy were read from the
    official documentation, not measured against a live account:
    [Webhooks](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/integrations/webhooks),
    [Event Types and Fields](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/integrations/webhooks/event-types-and-fields),
    [Sample Events](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/integrations/webhooks/sample-events)
    and the [REST API v1](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/api-v1). The three
    webhook pages are vendored in `vendor/` with their sha256 pinned by a
    test, and the SDK's list of event types is compared against them.

## The minimal path

One file with the inbox model, your product's subscription table, the handler
that applies an event, and the route:

```python
# src/billing.py
from datetime import datetime

from fastapi import FastAPI
from sqlalchemy import String, select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import register_exception_handlers
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import (
    AsyncDatabaseManager,
    BaseModel,
    BaseWebhookEventModel,
    UtcDateTime,
    WebhookInbox,
)
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.subscriptions.revenuecat import (
    RevenueCatWebhook,
    make_revenuecat_webhook_router,
    normalize,
)
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.settings import DatabaseSettings, RevenueCatSettings


class Settings(DatabaseSettings, RevenueCatSettings):
    """Database + RevenueCat credentials, read from the environment."""


class WebhookEventModel(BaseWebhookEventModel):
    """Webhook inbox: one row per distinct event."""

    __tablename__ = "webhook_events"


class SubscriptionModel(BaseModel):
    """Current subscription state of each app user."""

    __tablename__ = "subscriptions"

    app_user_id: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(255), unique=True)
    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(32))
    product_id: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(255), nullable=True)
    period_end: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(UtcDateTime, nullable=True)


settings = Settings()
db = AsyncDatabaseManager(**settings.database_kwargs())
inbox: WebhookInbox[WebhookEventModel] = WebhookInbox(db, model=WebhookEventModel)


async def apply_event(event: WebhookEventModel, session: AsyncSession) -> None:
    """Store the state the event left, in the inbox's own transaction.

    Args:
        event (WebhookEventModel): The claimed inbox row.
        session (AsyncSession): The session that also marks the event
            processed.
    """
    snapshot = normalize(RevenueCatWebhook.model_validate(event.payload).event)
    if snapshot.app_user_id is None:
        return
    current = (
        await session.execute(
            select(SubscriptionModel).where(
                SubscriptionModel.app_user_id == snapshot.app_user_id
            )
        )
    ).scalar_one_or_none()
    if current is None:
        current = SubscriptionModel(app_user_id=snapshot.app_user_id)
        session.add(current)
    current.status = snapshot.status.value
    current.product_id = snapshot.product_id
    current.period_end = snapshot.period_end


app = FastAPI()
register_exception_handlers(app)
app.include_router(
    make_revenuecat_webhook_router(
        inbox=inbox,
        secret=settings.REVENUECAT_WEBHOOK_SECRET,
    )
)
```

And the sweep that processes what arrived, every 5 minutes:

```python
# src/tasks/billing.py
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import CronEnum, TaskQueue

from src.billing import apply_event, db, inbox

tq = TaskQueue.rabbitmq("amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/", resources=[db])


@tq.cron(CronEnum.EVERY_5_MINUTES)
async def sweep_webhook_inbox() -> None:
    """Process every inbox event that is due."""
    await inbox.drain_once(apply_event)
```

In the RevenueCat dashboard, under **Integrations → Webhooks**, point the URL
at `https://<your-host>/webhooks/revenuecat` and fill the *authorization
header* field with the same value as `REVENUECAT_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.

What happens to a delivery, run with the code above (SQLite, three POSTs of a
trial `INITIAL_PURCHASE` carrying an `$email` in `subscriber_attributes` — no
header, with the header, with the header again —, one `drain_once`, then the
`subscriptions` row and the inbox row printed: status, and whether the stored
payload has `subscriber_attributes`):

```text
401 {'detail': 'Invalid RevenueCat webhook credentials', 'code': 'UNAUTHORIZED', 'details': {}}
200 {'recorded': True, 'event_id': 'evt-1'}
200 {'recorded': False, 'event_id': 'evt-1'}
processed 1 retrying 0
user-1 trial monthly 2030-03-17 17:46:40+00:00
processed False
```

The repeat got `200` with `recorded: False`: RevenueCat only needs to stop
retrying, and nothing was stored twice.

## Piece by piece

### 1. The route holds no business logic

`make_revenuecat_webhook_router` authenticates, records the event in the inbox
with `provider="revenuecat"` and `external_id=event.id`, and answers `200`.
That is all.

Why: according to the [documentation](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/integrations/webhooks),
any status other than `200` is a failure, RevenueCat retries "up to 5 times"
(after 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 minutes) and disconnects after 60 seconds. The
same page recommends deferring processing until after the response.

!!! tip "Process right away, without waiting for the sweep"
    Pass `on_recorded`: it receives the inbox row id of every **new** event
    (not of a repeat). Enqueue the task there. If enqueueing fails, the route
    still answers `200` — the event is already recorded and the sweep picks
    it up.

    ```python
    from uuid import UUID

    from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.subscriptions.revenuecat import (
        make_revenuecat_webhook_router,
    )
    from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import TaskQueue

    from src.billing import apply_event, inbox

    tq = TaskQueue.rabbitmq("amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/")


    @tq.task
    async def process_webhook_event(event_id: str) -> None:
        """Process one inbox event.

        Args:
            event_id (str): The inbox row id.
        """
        await inbox.process(UUID(event_id), apply_event)


    async def enqueue(event_id: UUID) -> None:
        """Send the newly recorded event to the worker.

        Args:
            event_id (UUID): The inbox row id.
        """
        await process_webhook_event.enqueue(str(event_id))


    router = make_revenuecat_webhook_router(
        inbox=inbox, secret="dashboard-value", on_recorded=enqueue
    )
    ```

### 2. Authentication: the header and, optionally, HMAC

RevenueCat offers two ways, both documented on the webhooks page:

| Way | Header | What it proves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Authorization header* (the value you type in the dashboard) | `Authorization` | that the sender knows the secret |
| *HMAC webhook signing* (opt-in, per integration) | `X-RevenueCat-Webhook-Signature: t=<ts>,v1=<hex>` | that **and** that the body is intact |

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.subscriptions.revenuecat import (
    make_revenuecat_webhook_router,
)
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.settings import RevenueCatSettings

from src.billing import inbox

settings = RevenueCatSettings()
router = make_revenuecat_webhook_router(
    inbox=inbox,
    secret=settings.REVENUECAT_WEBHOOK_SECRET,
    signing_secret=settings.REVENUECAT_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET,
)
```

A secret is configured when it holds a value. Every filled secret is
checked, and with both filled a delivery must pass both; an empty one only
turns its own check off. That is why the same code serves "header only",
"HMAC only" and "both", changing nothing but the environment variables.
Rules the SDK applies and the tests pin:

- constant-time comparison (`hmac.compare_digest`);
- the `Authorization` header is accepted with or without a `Bearer ` prefix;
- **no filled secret refuses everything** (`401`) — a forgotten environment
  variable does not turn into an open endpoint;
- `secret=None` together with `signing_secret=None` raises `ValueError` when
  the router is built: there is no unauthenticated route;
- an HMAC signature outside the 5-minute window is refused. According to the
  documentation, `t` is recomputed on every attempt, retries included, so the
  window only covers clock skew and latency.

!!! info "Per-request secret"
    `secret` and `signing_secret` also accept a `Callable[[Request], str]` —
    useful for rotation or for a service with several RevenueCat projects.
    Emptiness is read per request: a function returning `""` turns that
    check off for that delivery only.

### 3. The inbox: once, with an attempt budget

`WebhookInbox` is generic — it knows nothing about RevenueCat. It works the
same for Stripe, OpenPix, Mercado Pago or zap-api: record with the event id
the provider promises is stable across retries.

| Step | What it does | Why this way |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `record(provider, external_id, event_type, payload)` | `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` (PostgreSQL and SQLite) | a repeat returns `None` instead of raising |
| `claim(id)` | `UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'received'` | of two workers, only one wins |
| `process(id, handler)` | runs the handler **in the transaction** that marks it `processed` | the database effect and the mark commit together, or neither does |
| `fail(id, error)` | back to `received` with exponential backoff | a dependency that is down gets time to come back |
| `max_attempts` | once reached, the row is `failed` and leaves the sweep | a poisoned event does not run forever |
| `reclaim_stale()` | a row stuck in `processing` comes back (or fails, with no budget left) | a worker that died mid-way does not strand the event |

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import WebhookInbox

from src.billing import WebhookEventModel, db

inbox: WebhookInbox[WebhookEventModel] = WebhookInbox(
    db,
    model=WebhookEventModel,
    max_attempts=5,
    backoff_base_seconds=60.0,
    stale_after=600.0,
)
```

!!! warning "Effects outside the database are not in the transaction"
    E-mail, push, a call to another API: if the handler does that and then
    fails, the next attempt does it again. Make that effect idempotent on
    `event.external_id`.

An event that reached `failed` stays in the table for a person to look at
(`last_error` says why). To reprocess it after fixing the cause, set `status`
back to `received` and reset `attempts`.

### 4. From event to state: `normalize`

The documentation lists 21 event types. `normalize(event)` returns a
`SubscriptionSnapshot` with a `SubscriptionStatusEnum` and the fields that
matter (`app_user_id`, `product_id`, `entitlement_ids`, `period_end`,
`grace_period_end`, `reason`, `event_at`...):

| Event | Status |
| --- | --- |
| `INITIAL_PURCHASE`, `RENEWAL`, `UNCANCELLATION`, `NON_RENEWING_PURCHASE`, `PRODUCT_CHANGE`, `SUBSCRIPTION_EXTENDED`, `REFUND_REVERSED` | `TRIAL` when `period_type` is `TRIAL`, `ACTIVE` otherwise |
| `CANCELLATION` with `CUSTOMER_SUPPORT` | `REFUNDED` |
| `CANCELLATION` with `BILLING_ERROR`, `BILLING_ISSUE` | `BILLING_ISSUE` |
| `CANCELLATION` (any other reason) | `CANCELLED` — the period runs to its end |
| `SUBSCRIPTION_PAUSED` | `PAUSE_SCHEDULED` — the documentation says **not** to revoke access here |
| `EXPIRATION` with `SUBSCRIPTION_PAUSED` | `PAUSED` |
| `EXPIRATION` | `EXPIRED` |
| `TEMPORARY_ENTITLEMENT_GRANT` | `TEMPORARY_GRANT` (up to 24 h, during a store outage) |
| `TEST`, `TRANSFER`, `EXPERIMENT_ENROLLMENT`, `VIRTUAL_CURRENCY_TRANSACTION`, `SUBSCRIBER_ALIAS`, `PURCHASE_REDEEMED`, `INVOICE_ISSUANCE`, `PRICE_INCREASE_CONSENT_*` | `NO_CHANGE` |
| a type this release does not know | `UNKNOWN` — never raises |

What each status **means** for your product (which plan unlocks what, how long
the grace period lasts, what a refund takes away) stays in your service. The
SDK delivers the state, not the entitlement.

!!! tip "Out-of-order delivery"
    `snapshot.event_at` is when RevenueCat generated the event. Keep the last
    one applied per user and ignore an older event that arrives late.

### 5. Minimal collection

`subscriber_attributes` is where the app puts `$email`, a phone number and
whatever else it attached to the customer — the documentation's
`INITIAL_PURCHASE` sample carries an `$email`. It is still readable as
`event.subscriber_attributes`, but it stays **out of `model_dump()`**, and
`model_dump()` is what the route stores in the inbox. In the run above, the
`processed False` on the last line is exactly that: the field never reached
the database.

### 6. Reconciliation through the API

The [webhooks page](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/integrations/webhooks)
recommends re-reading the customer through `GET /subscribers` after any
webhook. `RevenueCatClient.get_subscriber` makes that call with a **secret**
key:

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import HTTPClient
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.subscriptions.revenuecat import (
    RevenueCatClient,
)
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.settings import RevenueCatSettings


async def main() -> None:
    """Read a user's current state straight from RevenueCat."""
    settings = RevenueCatSettings()
    async with HTTPClient(**settings.revenuecat_kwargs()) as http:
        info = await RevenueCatClient(http).get_subscriber("user-1456")
    for name, entitlement in info.subscriber.entitlements.items():
        print(name, entitlement.expires_date)


asyncio.run(main())
```

!!! danger "The endpoint is *Get or Create*"
    The reference calls the route "Get or Create Customer": an `app_user_id`
    RevenueCat has never seen is **created**. Reconcile only ids that came
    from a webhook or from your own users table. That is also why
    `tempest integrations verify revenuecat` exits with code 2 without calling
    anything: verifying the key through that route would create a customer.

The `app_user_id` reaches the path encoded as a single segment, and `""`,
`"."` and `".."` raise `ValueError` before any request — the dot is not
escaped, and up to v0.334.1 `".."` climbed one level up the path with the
secret key. `FakeRevenueCatClient` refuses the same three.

For tests, `FakeRevenueCatClient` answers what you seed and fails when told
to:

```python
import asyncio

import httpx

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.testing.fakes import FakeRevenueCatClient


async def main() -> None:
    """Seed a customer, read it, and force a network failure."""
    fake = FakeRevenueCatClient()
    fake.set_subscriber("user-1", {"entitlements": {"pro": {}}})
    info = await fake.get_subscriber("user-1")
    print(list(info.subscriber.entitlements))

    fake.fail_next(httpx.ConnectError("down"))
    try:
        await fake.get_subscriber("user-1")
    except httpx.ConnectError as exc:
        print("failed:", exc)


asyncio.run(main())
```

```text
['pro']
failed: down
```

An `app_user_id` nobody seeded raises `httpx.HTTPStatusError` (404), the same
type the real client raises for a non-2xx answer — instead of creating the
customer as the real endpoint would.

## Configuration

| Variable | What for | Empty means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `REVENUECAT_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | the dashboard's *authorization header* value | the `Authorization` header is not checked; with `REVENUECAT_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET` empty too, every delivery is refused (`401`) |
| `REVENUECAT_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET` | the HMAC secret, when enabled | the signature is not checked; with `REVENUECAT_WEBHOOK_SECRET` empty too, every delivery is refused (`401`) |
| `REVENUECAT_API_KEY` | secret key (`sk_...`) for `GET /v1/subscribers` | the call goes out with an empty `Bearer `; the reference documents `401` for an invalid key |

Composed with `EnvironmentSettings`, `RevenueCatSettings` fails the boot under
`ENV=production` when **neither** webhook secret is set — in production that
would mean refusing every purchase and renewal:

```text
ValidationError 1 validation error for Settings
  Value error, ENV=production refuses development values:
- REVENUECAT_WEBHOOK_SECRET: empty, so every RevenueCat webhook is refused
```

## RevenueCat switched off (`REVENUECAT_ENABLED=false`)

`REVENUECAT_ENABLED=false` makes the production guard skip the
both-secrets-empty rule and puts `"revenuecat"` in
`settings.disabled_integrations()`. That is all: the webhook dependency
reads the secrets, not the flag, so with both empty it keeps refusing
every delivery with `401` — nothing is accepted silently. See
[Switching integrations on and off](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/system-checks.md#switching-integrations-on-and-off-phased-deploys).

## Recap

- `make_revenuecat_webhook_router` authenticates, records in the inbox and
  answers `200`; every filled secret is checked, and with none filled every
  delivery is refused.
- `WebhookInbox` records each event once, processes it under a claim, commits
  the effect with the mark, and stops at `max_attempts` — and works for any
  provider.
- `normalize` turns the 21 event types into one state; a new type becomes
  `UNKNOWN`.
- `subscriber_attributes` is not stored.
- `RevenueCatClient.get_subscriber` reconciles — remembering that the endpoint
  creates the customer when it does not exist.

Source: https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/deploy-safety.md

# Safe deploys (migrations + graceful shutdown)

Two classic deploy risks: a migration that **deletes data** by accident,
and a rollout that **severs in-flight requests** when the old pod dies.
This recipe covers the two defenses the SDK ships.

## Safe migrations: `safe_upgrade`

`AlembicHelper.safe_upgrade()` runs the upgrade **only if** no pending
migration is destructive. It scans each pending revision's `def upgrade()`
for data-deleting calls — `op.drop_table`, `op.drop_column`,
`op.drop_constraint` (and `batch_op` variants) — and, if it finds one,
raises `DestructiveMigrationError` **without touching the database**.
`sync_schema()` uses the same guard, except on an empty database (no stamp and
no application table), where there is no data to lose and the whole tree runs —
see [Migrations](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/migrations.md#the-three-states-it-tells-apart).

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AlembicHelper, DestructiveMigrationError


def deploy_migrations() -> None:
    """Apply migrations on deploy, blocking accidental DROPs."""
    helper: AlembicHelper = AlembicHelper(db_url="postgresql+asyncpg://...")
    try:
        helper.safe_upgrade("head")
    except DestructiveMigrationError as exc:
        # CI/CD fails here — someone must review and unblock with force.
        for revision, op in exc.offences:
            print(f"blocked: {revision} → {op}")
        raise
```

The scan looks at the migration **code**, not the generated SQL — so it
never false-positives on the table rebuild SQLite does in batch mode. A
`drop_*` in `downgrade()` (the normal, expected path) is ignored.

### Allowing an intentional DROP

When the DROP is intentional (you took a backup, you reviewed it), pass
`force=True` — the destructive operations are logged and the upgrade runs:

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AlembicHelper

helper: AlembicHelper = AlembicHelper(db_url="postgresql+asyncpg://...")
helper.safe_upgrade("head", force=True)  # I know what I'm doing
```

!!! tip "Inspect only"
    `helper.pending_destructive_ops("head")` returns the list of
    `(revision, operation)` without running anything — handy for a CI step
    that only reports.

!!! danger "force=True deletes data"
    `DROP COLUMN` / `DROP TABLE` are irreversible. Only use `force=True`
    after a backup and human review.

## Back up before migrating (`DatabaseBackup`)

`safe_upgrade` refuses the destructive migration, but sometimes the DROP is
intentional. The right order then is backup → `force=True` → verify.
`DatabaseBackup` dumps from the very same `DATABASE_URL` the service uses:

```python
# scripts/deploy.py
from pathlib import Path

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import DatabaseBackup

from src.core.settings import settings

backup: DatabaseBackup = DatabaseBackup(settings.DATABASE_URL)
written: Path = backup.backup()
print(f"dump written to {written}")
```

The `+asyncpg` / `+aiosqlite` suffix is stripped for you — you pass the
application URL and keep no second variable just for backups. Without
`output=`, the file lands in `backups/<db>_<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>.<ext>`.

A dump is a full copy of the database, so only its owner can read it: the
file is created with mode `0600` (whatever the umask) and a directory
`backup()` creates gets `0700`. A `tempest new` project already lists
`backups/`, `*.dump` and `*.sqlite` in `.gitignore` and `.dockerignore`; in
an older project, add those lines to both files.

| Backend | `backup()` uses | Format |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `postgresql` | `pg_dump` | custom (`-Fc`) by default; a `.sql` `output` (or `plain=True`) writes a text dump |
| `sqlite` | file copy | the `.sqlite` file itself |

Restoring mirrors it — the format comes from the extension:

```python
from pathlib import Path

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import DatabaseBackup

from src.core.settings import settings

backup = DatabaseBackup(settings.DATABASE_URL)


backup.restore(Path("backups/app_20260727-104500.dump"))
```

`clean=True` (default) drops existing objects before recreating, so the restore
is a faithful copy: `pg_restore --clean --if-exists` for the custom format,
`DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE` ahead of `psql -f` for plain, file overwrite for
SQLite. Pass `clean=False` to restore **on top of** an existing database.

### Database in a container: `docker_container=`

When Postgres runs in its own container, installing `postgresql-client` in the
application image — and keeping it on a version compatible with the server — is
dead weight carried for a nightly job. The database image already ships the
`pg_dump` that matches it exactly:

```python
from pathlib import Path

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import DatabaseBackup

from src.core.settings import settings

backup = DatabaseBackup(settings.DATABASE_URL, docker_container="app-db")

written: Path = backup.backup(Path("backups/app.dump"))
backup.restore(written)
```

With `docker_container` set, `pg_dump` runs **inside** the container and the
dump comes back over stdout into the local file; restore goes the other way,
with the file fed to `pg_restore`/`psql` on stdin. Without it, nothing changes.

!!! note "Three details that make this mode work"
    - **`-h`/`-p` are dropped.** The URL's host and port describe how the
      *application* reaches the database from outside; inside the container that
      route does not exist. User and database still come from the URL.
    - **The password crosses by name.** The command carries `-e PGPASSWORD`
      with no value: Docker copies it from the calling process's environment.
      Spelling it `-e PGPASSWORD=…` would put the password in the container's
      command line, where any `ps` on the host reads it.
    - **Nothing is copied in.** Restore streams over stdin instead of
      `docker cp`, so no temporary file is left inside the container and there
      is no window where one sits there half written.

    What the mode does require is `docker` on the caller's `PATH` — and that is
    what `BackupToolMissingError` checks here, in place of `pg_dump`.

!!! warning "The two errors you will hit first"
    - `BackupToolMissingError` — `pg_dump` / `pg_restore` / `psql` (or `docker`,
      in the mode above) is not on `PATH`. An app container rarely ships the
      Postgres client; install `postgresql-client` in the image that runs the
      deploy, use `docker_container=`, or run the backup elsewhere.
    - `UnsupportedBackupBackendError` — a dialect with no strategy (MySQL, SQL
      Server). Only Postgres and SQLite are covered.

    Both are raised **before** `backups/` is created, so a failure never leaves
    an empty directory behind for someone to mistake for a finished backup.

!!! info "Synchronous on purpose"
    `pg_dump` is a process and a file copy is disk I/O — neither gains anything
    from `async`. Call these from a CLI command or a deploy script; from async
    code, use `asyncio.to_thread(backup.backup)`.

## Graceful shutdown: drain in-flight requests

On rollout, the orchestrator sends `SIGTERM` and, after a while, `SIGKILL`.
If a request is still running when the worker dies, it is severed — an
intermittent 502. `GracefulShutdownMiddleware`:

1. Once **draining**, replies `503` + `Retry-After` to new requests —
   including the health endpoint, which is what makes the load balancer stop
   routing to this pod.
2. **Counts** in-flight requests; `wait_drained()` waits for them to finish
   (with a timeout).

### What uvicorn already does on its own on `SIGTERM`

Before choosing where to trigger draining, look at what happens under
uvicorn. Measured with uvicorn in a subprocess, a 3 s request in flight and
`SIGTERM` 0.5 s later:

```text
after SIGTERM: /health ConnectError
in-flight /slow: 200
LIFESPAN-SHUTDOWN in_flight=0
LIFESPAN-DRAINED True
```

uvicorn **closes the listener right away** (the new request does not even
connect), **waits itself** for the in-flight request to finish, and only
**then** runs the lifespan shutdown. So a `begin_drain()` in the lifespan
shutdown arrives when no request is left — it never emits a `503`, and
`wait_drained()` returns `True` immediately. Under uvicorn, the wait for
in-flight requests is uvicorn's own, bounded by
`--timeout-graceful-shutdown`.

### Drain **before** `SIGTERM`

The `503` is only useful if it goes out while the listener still accepts
connections — that is, before `SIGTERM`. On Kubernetes that moment is the
`preStop` hook, which runs before the signal. Bind draining to a signal
uvicorn does **not** use (`SIGUSR1`) and send it from `preStop`:

```python
import signal

from fastapi import FastAPI
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import GracefulShutdownMiddleware

shutdown: GracefulShutdownMiddleware = GracefulShutdownMiddleware(drain_timeout=25.0)

app: FastAPI = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware, dispatch=shutdown.dispatch)
shutdown.install_signal_handlers((signal.SIGUSR1,))


@app.get("/health")
async def health() -> dict[str, str]:
    """Readiness: answers 503 as soon as draining starts."""
    return {"status": "ok"}
```

```yaml
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec:
      command: ["sh", "-c", "kill -USR1 1 && sleep 15"]
```

Measured with the same app, sending `SIGUSR1` before `SIGTERM`:

```text
after SIGUSR1: /health 503 Retry-After= 5
after SIGTERM: /health ConnectError
in-flight /slow: 200
```

After `SIGUSR1`, every new request gets `503` with `Retry-After` — the
readiness probe fails and the pod leaves the load balancer — while the
in-flight request finishes with `200`. The `preStop` `sleep` gives that time
to happen; `SIGTERM` arrives afterwards, and uvicorn waits for whatever is
still in flight.

!!! warning "One process per pod"
    `kill -USR1 1` reaches the container's PID 1 — your `python main.py`
    when `CMD` uses the exec form. With `uvicorn --workers N`, PID 1 is the
    supervisor and the signal never reaches the workers; in that case run
    one worker per pod, or signal each worker.

!!! info "`install_signal_handlers` needs the main thread"
    `signal.signal` only works on the main thread; elsewhere the method does
    nothing. The measurement above calls the method at module level in a
    `main.py` started with `uvicorn.run(app)`. Do not pass `SIGTERM` or
    `SIGINT`: those belong to uvicorn.

Set the orchestrator's grace period (`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`) above
the `preStop` `sleep` plus uvicorn's `--timeout-graceful-shutdown`.

## Recap

- `AlembicHelper.safe_upgrade()` refuses destructive migrations
  (`DestructiveMigrationError`); `force=True` allows them;
  `pending_destructive_ops()` only inspects.
- `DatabaseBackup(url).backup()` / `.restore(path)` — per-dialect dump and
  restore (Postgres via `pg_dump`/`pg_restore`, SQLite by file copy) off the
  service's own `DATABASE_URL`.
- `GracefulShutdownMiddleware` replies `503` while draining and
  `wait_drained()` waits for in-flight requests. Under uvicorn, trigger
  draining **before** `SIGTERM` (`install_signal_handlers((signal.SIGUSR1,))`
  + `preStop`): by the lifespan shutdown the listener is already closed and
  there is no request left to refuse.
