| Who moves the bytes | the Python process | nginx |
| Needs nginx in front | no | yes, with the internal `location` below |
| `206` / `304` | answered by the SDK | answered by the bucket, behind nginx |
| Good for | small files, local dev, deploys without nginx | video, large files, high traffic |

#### Switch it by configuration

Both modes come out of **the same route**. `serve_object` picks according to
what the client got in its constructor, and `StorageSettings` maps two new
variables:

```bash
# .env
STORAGE_ENDPOINT=bucket:9000          # INTERNAL endpoint: the SDK signs against it
STORAGE_ACCEL_REDIRECT=true         # false (default) = proxy through the app
STORAGE_ACCEL_PREFIX=/_bucket/      # nginx's internal location
```

```python
from fastapi import APIRouter, Request
from starlette.responses import Response
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AsyncMinIOClient, guess_media_type

from src.core.settings import settings

router = APIRouter()
storage = AsyncMinIOClient(**settings.storage_kwargs())


@router.get("/files/{key:path}")
async def download_file(key: str, request: Request) -> Response:
    """Authorise and deliver — through the app or through nginx, per the .env."""
    return await storage.serve_object(
        key,
        request=request,
        media_type=guess_media_type(key),
        as_attachment=False,
    )
```

!!! warning "In redirect mode, `inline` needs `media_type=`"
    `accel_redirect_response` makes no `stat`, so it does not know which type
    the bucket will answer with. Without `media_type=`, `as_attachment=False`
    comes out `attachment`. With it, the type is signed into the URL (the
    bucket answers with that one, not the stored one) and only becomes
    `inline` if it is in `INLINE_SAFE_MEDIA_TYPES`. `guess_media_type(key)`
    above resolves it from the key's extension: `lesson.mp4` goes inline,
    `page.html` becomes a download. `accel_redirect_response` defaults to
    `as_attachment=True`. `media_type=` goes through the same check as
    `presigned_get_url`: a bare `type/subtype`, with no parameter, comma or
    line break — anything else raises `ValueError` before anything is signed.

With `STORAGE_ACCEL_REDIRECT=false`, it is the previous section's
`download_response`. With `true`, it is `accel_redirect_response`, and the
`request` is not used: nginx forwards the client's `Range` and
`If-None-Match` to the bucket by itself.

!!! info "`accel_redirect_response` directly"
    Want the redirect on a single route, regardless of the flag? Call
    `storage.accel_redirect_response(key, internal_prefix="/_bucket/",
    expires=timedelta(minutes=5), filename=..., media_type=...,
    as_attachment=False, cache_control=...)`. It **never** uses
    `STORAGE_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT`: the URL is signed against `STORAGE_ENDPOINT`, the
    host nginx is going to call.

#### The nginx block

```nginx
upstream app {
    server app:8000;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name example.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://app;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
    }

    location /_bucket/ {
        internal;
        proxy_pass http://bucket:9000/;
        proxy_set_header Host bucket:9000;
        proxy_hide_header X-Content-Type-Options;
        add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;
        add_header Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'none'; sandbox" always;
        add_header Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy "same-site" always;
    }
}
```

Each line of `location /_bucket/` has a reason:

- **`internal;`** — only nginx gets in here, following an
  `X-Accel-Redirect`. A client asking for `/_bucket/...` directly gets `404`.
- **`proxy_pass http://bucket:9000/;` with the trailing slash** — with the
  slash, nginx replaces the `/_bucket/` prefix with `/`, and the bucket
  receives `/media/lesson.mp4?X-Amz-...`, exactly the path that was signed.
  Without it, the prefix goes along, MinIO reads `_bucket` as the bucket name
  and answers `400 InvalidBucketName`.
- **`proxy_set_header Host bucket:9000;`** — the SigV4 signature covers
  `Host`. It has to be the `STORAGE_ENDPOINT` that signed the URL. The danger is
  inheritance: a `proxy_set_header` defined at `server` level (the
  `Host $host` nearly every config has for the app) is inherited by any
  `location` that defines none. The bucket then receives
  `Host: example.com` and answers `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch` — the symptom is
  "the file does not load".
- **The `add_header ... always` lines** — the security headers of every
  download, and this is the only place they reach the client from. nginx
  answers with the bucket's response, not the app's empty one: a header the
  app put there would not get through (measured — which is why the SDK does
  not set them). Without `always`, nginx adds the header to only part of
  the statuses — that is how the `add_header` documentation defines it.
- **`proxy_hide_header X-Content-Type-Options;`** — MinIO already sends
  `nosniff`; without hiding its own, the client gets `nosniff, nosniff`
  (measured). Hiding and re-emitting leaves a single value, whatever storage
  sits behind.

!!! warning "`Content-Type` and `Content-Disposition` travel inside the URL"
    The SDK does not put those headers on the empty response: it signs them
    into the URL as the S3 `response-content-type`,
    `response-content-disposition` and `response-cache-control` overrides, and
    the bucket returns them along with the bytes. Measured on nginx 1.27.5:
    the bucket's `Content-Type` wins over the one the app sets, and a
    `Content-Disposition` set on both reaches the client twice.

!!! danger "Without nginx in front, the flag leaks the signed URL"
    With `STORAGE_ACCEL_REDIRECT=true` and no nginx intercepting, the client
    gets an empty `200` carrying the `X-Accel-Redirect` — path and signature
    included. The URL points at the internal host and is valid for `expires`
    (5 minutes by default). Only turn the flag on where the block above is
    deployed.

#### What was measured

`tests/storage/test_accel_redirect_live.py` (`make test-docker`) starts
MinIO and nginx in containers and the app under uvicorn, and downloads
through the route. The same file passed in full on nginx 1.22.1, 1.27.5 and
1.29.8:

| Request | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /files/clip.mp4` | `200`, the object's bytes, the `Content-Type` stored in the bucket |
| `GET /files/clip.mp4` with `Range: bytes=100-199` | `206`, `Content-Range: bytes 100-199/1048576` |
| `GET /files/clip.mp4` with `If-None-Match: <etag>` | `304` |
| key with a space, an accent and `+` | `200` |
| `GET /_bucket/media/clip.mp4` straight from the client | `404` |
| a `location` inheriting `Host $host` | `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch` |
| `proxy_pass` without the trailing slash | `400 InvalidBucketName` |
| `GET /files/clip.mp4`, `location` with the `add_header` lines | `X-Content-Type-Options`, CSP and CORP, one value each |
| `location` without the `add_header` lines | `200` with no CSP nor CORP, even with the app setting both on the empty response |
| `as_attachment=False` with no `media_type=` | `Content-Disposition: attachment` |
| the same route with `STORAGE_ACCEL_REDIRECT=false` and `Range: bytes=-10` | `206` from the app |

In the test, bucket, app and nginx run on the host network, so the internal
endpoint is `127.0.0.1:<port>` instead of `bucket:9000`. What matters is the
same: the `Host` nginx sends is the host that signed the URL.

### Private file behind a signed URL of your own route

When the frontend talks only to the backend, a private file needs a URL **of
the backend** that the browser can open on its own. `<img src>`,
`<video src>` and a download link send no `Authorization: Bearer`, and a
session cookie across the app's domain and the API's runs into `SameSite`.
The bucket's presigned URL does not help: it sends the browser to the bucket,
not to your route.

The way out has the same shape as a presigned URL, aimed at the app's route.
The mapper that already authorized the caller builds
`/api/files/<key>?expires=<ts>&signature=<mac>` with `sign_path`, and the
route checks the signature with `make_signed_path_dependency` before
streaming:

```python
from datetime import timedelta

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Request
from starlette.responses import Response
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    AsyncMinIOClient,
    BaseSchema,
    make_signed_path_dependency,
    register_exception_handlers,
    sign_path,
)

FILES_SECRET: str = "replace-with-settings.JWT_SECRET"
FILES_PURPOSE: str = "files"

storage = AsyncMinIOClient(
    endpoint="minio.internal:9000",
    access_key="minioadmin",
    secret_key="minioadmin",
    default_bucket="uploads",
)
signed_file = make_signed_path_dependency(secret=FILES_SECRET, purpose=FILES_PURPOSE)


class AttachmentResponseSchema(BaseSchema):
    """An attachment as the frontend gets it: the key and a URL to open."""

    key: str
    url: str


def to_attachment_response(key: str) -> AttachmentResponseSchema:
    """Map the stored key to the schema, with the URL already signed."""
    return AttachmentResponseSchema(
        key=key,
        url=sign_path(
            f"/api/files/{key}",
            secret=FILES_SECRET,
            expires_in=timedelta(minutes=15),
            purpose=FILES_PURPOSE,
        ),
    )


app = FastAPI()
register_exception_handlers(app)


@app.get("/api/attachments/{key:path}")
async def get_attachment(key: str) -> AttachmentResponseSchema:
    """Your authorization goes here: JWT, resource owner, role."""
    return to_attachment_response(key)


@app.get("/api/files/{key:path}", dependencies=[Depends(signed_file)])
async def download_file(key: str, request: Request) -> Response:
    """Only reached with a signed URL that has not expired."""
    return await storage.download_response(
        key, request=request, as_attachment=False
    )
```

Signed at 12:00 UTC on October 1st 2026 with the secret above, the `url` the
frontend receives for the key `aulas/aula 01.mp4` is:

```text
/api/files/aulas/aula%2001.mp4?expires=1790856900&signature=e9vPzlJkaaLXY6fJ0dSsV6RS6D3pOElruFdeskdikck
```

It goes straight into the tag, with no header at all:

```html
<video src="/api/files/aulas/aula%2001.mp4?expires=1790856900&signature=e9vPzlJkaaLXY6fJ0dSsV6RS6D3pOElruFdeskdikck" controls></video>
```

Piece by piece:

- **`sign_path` in the mapper.** It runs after authorization, so only a caller
  allowed to see the attachment ever gets the URL. Whoever holds the URL opens
  the file until `expires` — it is a capability, like a presigned URL, which
  is why the window is short.
- **`make_signed_path_dependency` on the route.** The dependency reads
  `expires` and `signature` from the query and checks them against the
  decoded request path. The handler only runs for a valid signature that has
  not expired: the bucket is not even consulted for a rejected URL.
- **`download_response(..., request=)` is unchanged.** `Range` goes through
  the signature, so the `<video>` still seeks and a download still resumes.
  Swap in `serve_object` and the same dependency guards the
  `X-Accel-Redirect` mode from the previous section.

`tests/storage/test_signed_url_live.py` (`make test-docker`) builds this route
against MinIO in a container and measures: `200` with the whole object through
the signed URL, `206` with `Range: bytes=1000-1999` and only that slice, and
`403` for a tampered or unsigned URL, with no `stat_object` reaching the
bucket. With `serve_object` and `accel_redirect=True`, the signed URL answers
the `X-Accel-Redirect` and the tampered one answers `403` without it.

#### What the signature covers

- **The path and `expires`.** The signature is
  `HMAC-SHA256(key, "<expires>\n<path>")`. Changing the object key or
  stretching `expires` breaks the MAC. Other query parameters are **not**
  covered.
- **The `purpose`.** The MAC key is derived from the secret with the
  `purpose` (`HMAC-SHA256(secret, "tempest-fastapi-sdk.signed-url.v1\0" +
  purpose)`) and is never the raw secret. That is why reusing `JWT_SECRET` is
  safe, and why a URL signed for `"files"` does not open a route guarded with
  `"email-link"`.
- **Constant-time comparison**, with `hmac.compare_digest`.

| The request | Response |
| --- | --- |
| signed URL, not expired | the handler runs |
| `expires` changed | `403`, `code: "SIGNED_URL_INVALID"` |
| path changed | `403`, `code: "SIGNED_URL_INVALID"` |
| signed with another `purpose` or another secret | `403`, `code: "SIGNED_URL_INVALID"` |
| no `expires`/`signature`, or a non-numeric `expires` | `403`, `code: "SIGNED_URL_INVALID"` (never `422`) |
| authentic, but at the `expires` second or later | `403`, `code: "SIGNED_URL_EXPIRED"` |

Each row is a test in `tests/api/test_signed_path_dependency.py`. The body
follows the SDK envelope:

```json
{"detail": "Signed URL has expired", "code": "SIGNED_URL_EXPIRED", "details": {}}
```

!!! info "Why `403` and not `401`"
    A signed URL is a capability, not a login: no credential the client could
    send fixes the URL. S3 answers an expired or tampered presigned URL with
    `403` for the same reason. A `401` would also trip the "session expired,
    back to login" interceptor nearly every frontend installs, while the
    user's session is fine. The two `code`s exist so the frontend can tell
    "ask the backend for a fresh URL" (`SIGNED_URL_EXPIRED`) from "this link
    was tampered with" (`SIGNED_URL_INVALID`).

#### The path encoding rule

`sign_path` takes the **decoded** path, the way the route will see it in
`request.scope["path"]` (it is what `{key:path}` receives), and returns the
URL already percent-encoded. Starlette decodes the path before routing, so
both sides sign the same string:

- `aula 01.mp4` travels as `aula%2001.mp4`, `100%.pdf` as `100%25.pdf`, and
  `á.txt` as `%C3%A1.txt`; the route receives the original key;
- `/api/files/a%2Fb.pdf` and `/api/files/a/b.pdf` reach the route as the same
  path, with the same key `a/b.pdf`, and verify with the same signature.

Measured on Starlette 0.46.0 and on 1.6.0 — the floor `fastapi>=0.165.0`
requires today; the suite runs on 1.10.0.

!!! warning "Pass the decoded path, never an encoded one"
    `sign_path("/api/files/aula%2001.mp4", ...)` signs the literal key
    `aula%2001.mp4`, which becomes `aula%252001.mp4` in the URL. Build the
    path from the key as it is stored.

!!! tip "Mounted apps and `root_path`"
    Under `app.mount("/v1", sub_app)` the route sees `/v1/api/files/...`, so
    sign with the mount prefix. A proxy `root_path` (the prefix the reverse
    proxy strips before forwarding) does **not** show up in
    `request.scope["path"]`: sign without it and prepend the prefix to the
    URL the browser gets.

### Presigned URL — direct browser upload

Recommended pattern for large files: the client `PUT`s directly to MinIO/S3 and bytes don't pass through FastAPI.

```python
from datetime import timedelta
from uuid import uuid4

from fastapi import APIRouter
from pydantic import BaseModel

from src.api.app import storage

router = APIRouter()


class PresignedUploadResponse(BaseModel):
    key: str
    url: str


@router.post("/uploads/presign")
async def presign_upload() -> PresignedUploadResponse:
    """Return a temporary URL the client can PUT to directly."""
    key = f"uploads/{uuid4().hex}"
    url = await storage.presigned_put_url(key, expires=timedelta(minutes=15))
    return PresignedUploadResponse(key=key, url=url)
```

JS client:

```javascript
const { key, url } = await fetch("/uploads/presign", { method: "POST" }).then(r => r.json());
await fetch(url, { method: "PUT", body: file });
```

!!! warning "A signed `PUT` does not cap the size"
    Nothing about the body goes into a `PUT` signature: the client sends as
    many bytes as it likes and the service only learns the size after the
    upload. For a cap the store itself enforces, use `presigned_post_policy`
    (below).

### Direct upload with a cap — `presigned_post_policy`

An S3 form `POST` carries a signed *policy*. The key, the `Content-Type` and
the `content-length-range` condition go in it, and the **store** refuses
whatever falls outside, before storing anything:

```python
from uuid import uuid4

from fastapi import APIRouter

from src.api.app import storage
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import BaseSchema

router = APIRouter()

MAX_PHOTO_BYTES: int = 5 * 1024 * 1024


class PresignedFormResponse(BaseSchema):
    key: str
    url: str
    fields: dict[str, str]


@router.post("/uploads/photo")
async def presign_photo() -> PresignedFormResponse:
    """Return a form the store accepts only up to 5 MiB, as JPEG."""
    key = f"uploads/{uuid4().hex}.jpg"
    post = await storage.presigned_post_policy(
        key,
        max_bytes=MAX_PHOTO_BYTES,
        content_type="image/jpeg",
    )
    return PresignedFormResponse(key=key, url=post.url, fields=post.fields)
```

JS client — the fields first, the file **last** (S3 ignores whatever comes
after it):

```javascript
const { url, fields } = await fetch("/uploads/photo", { method: "POST" }).then(r => r.json());
const form = new FormData();
Object.entries(fields).forEach(([name, value]) => form.append(name, value));
form.append("file", file);
await fetch(url, { method: "POST", body: form });
```

Measured against MinIO `RELEASE.2025-04-22T22-12-26Z`
(`tests/storage/test_presign_live.py`):

| Upload | Store answer |
| --- | --- |
| within the cap | `204` |
| 1 byte over `max_bytes` | `400 EntityTooLarge` |
| under `min_bytes` | `400 EntityTooSmall` |
| another `Content-Type` or another `key` | `403 AccessDenied` |

Nothing is stored on a refusal.

!!! tip "Same shape on the local backend"
    `LocalObjectStorageClient.presigned_post_policy` returns the same
    `PresignedPost`, and the `make_local_storage_router` route enforces the
    same limits (`413`/`400`/`403`). The JavaScript above does not change
    when the service switches backend — see [Local storage](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/local-storage.md).

!!! info "The declared type is not the content"
    The `Content-Type` condition pins the **declared** type in the form,
    not the bytes. Before trusting the file, read its head on the server
    (`stream_object`) and check the format's signature.

### Presigned URL — temporary download

To serve private files without routing bytes through the API:

```python
from datetime import timedelta

from fastapi import APIRouter

from src.api.app import storage

router = APIRouter()


@router.get("/files/{key}/url")
async def get_download_url(key: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Download URL valid for 1 hour."""
    url = await storage.presigned_get_url(key, expires=timedelta(hours=1))
    return {"url": url}
```

#### With the type the server checked

`filename`, `media_type` and `as_attachment` go into the URL as S3
`response-*` overrides, **signed**: the store answers with them, and editing
any of them in the URL gives `403`. That serves the file with the type the
server checked, not the one the client declared on upload:

```python
from datetime import timedelta

from src.api.app import storage


async def photo_url(key: str) -> str:
    """Link that opens inline in an <img>, as JPEG, for 10 minutes."""
    return await storage.presigned_get_url(
        key,
        expires=timedelta(minutes=10),
        media_type="image/jpeg",
        as_attachment=False,
    )
```

`as_attachment=False` becomes `inline` only for a type safe to display
(`INLINE_SAFE_MEDIA_TYPES`); `text/html` and `image/svg+xml` stay
`attachment`. `media_type` takes a bare `type/subtype`, no parameters. With
none of the three, the link answers with what was stored, as before.

### Separate public endpoint for presigned URLs *(v0.88.0+)*

Common production shape: the backend talks to MinIO over a **fast private network** (`servus-storage:9000`, no TLS), but the **browser** can't reach that host — it needs a **public HTTPS** host. If you sign the presigned URL with the internal endpoint, the link carries `servus-storage:9000` and the browser can't open it.

Fix: `STORAGE_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT`. Presigned URLs (`presigned_get_url` / `presigned_put_url`) are then **signed against the public host**, while **every server→MinIO operation keeps using the internal endpoint**.

```bash
# .env
STORAGE_ENDPOINT=servus-storage:9000            # internal Docker network (ops)
STORAGE_SECURE=false
STORAGE_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT=https://storage.example.com   # browser (presigned)
# STORAGE_PUBLIC_SECURE=true                     # optional; https:// already implies it
```

!!! info "Why two clients, not a host replace"
    A presigned URL is SigV4-signed including the `Host` header. Rewriting the host **after** signing invalidates the signature. So the SDK keeps a second `minio.Minio` (same credentials) whose only job is to **sign** against the public host — the internal `AsyncMinIOClient.client` still does put/get/stat/ensure_bucket over the private network.

!!! tip "Without `STORAGE_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT`"
    Unchanged behaviour: presigned URLs are signed with `STORAGE_ENDPOINT` (single-endpoint mode). The split is fully opt-in.

The public host's proxy must route to the **MinIO S3 API (port 9000)** over TLS and forward the correct `Host` (the signature validates it).

### Batch operations — presign / upload / download *(v0.133.0+)*

**List** endpoints usually resolve **one key per row** — a page of profiles, each with its picture. Doing that in a `for` loop with `await presigned_get_url(...)` **serializes** the N thread hops (every `minio` call runs in `asyncio.to_thread`). The three batch methods fan the work out at once, under a concurrency ceiling:

- `presigned_get_urls(keys)` → `dict[str, str]` (key → URL)
- `put_objects(items)` → `dict[str, str]` (key → ETag)
- `get_objects_bytes(keys)` → `dict[str, bytes]` (key → payload)

```python
from fastapi import APIRouter

from src.api.app import storage

router = APIRouter()


@router.post("/files/urls")
async def sign_many(keys: list[str]) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Sign a page of keys in one call instead of one per request."""
    return await storage.presigned_get_urls(keys)
```

Duplicate keys are **collapsed** (each object is signed/fetched once), and the result is a `dict` — look each row up with `result.get(row.key)`.

!!! tip "In the service: `file_urls` for pages"
    If your service uses `StoredFileServiceMixin`, prefer `file_urls([...])` — the batch counterpart of `file_url`. It **drops `None`/empty keys** and returns a `dict`, ideal for building a page of responses:

    ```python
    users = [...]  # rows on the page
    urls = await user_service.file_urls([u.profile_picture for u in users])
    for user in users:
        user.profile_picture_url = urls.get(user.profile_picture)  # None if empty
    ```

!!! note "Fail-fast semantics"
    All three methods are **fail-fast**: the first failure aborts the batch and propagates (default `asyncio.gather`) — the same behavior as running the operations one by one. Need to tolerate partial failure? Run the items individually and handle each exception.

!!! info "Concurrency ceiling (`max_concurrency`, default 16)"
    Each operation is dispatched to a default-executor thread. Scheduling thousands at once saturates the pool and spikes memory. An `asyncio.Semaphore` bounds how many run at the same time while preserving order. Tune it via `max_concurrency=` (minimum 1; `0` or negative raises `ValueError`).

Batch upload uses `PutObjectItem`, which mirrors the per-object arguments of `put_object` (content type, metadata, length for streams):

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AsyncMinIOClient, PutObjectItem

from src.core.settings import settings

storage = AsyncMinIOClient(**settings.storage_kwargs())

# In your code these come off disk (`Path(...).read_bytes()`) or from the upload.
thumb_a = b"\xff\xd8\xff\xdb bytes of the first JPEG"
thumb_b = b"\xff\xd8\xff\xdb bytes of the second JPEG"


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    etags = await storage.put_objects(
        [
            PutObjectItem(key="thumbs/a.jpg", data=thumb_a, content_type="image/jpeg"),
            PutObjectItem(key="thumbs/b.jpg", data=thumb_b, content_type="image/jpeg"),
        ]
    )


asyncio.run(main())
```

!!! warning "`get_objects_bytes` loads everything in memory"
    Like `get_object_bytes`, the batch is for **small** objects — each payload becomes `bytes` in RAM. For large files, stream them individually with `stream_object`.

### List objects by prefix

```python
from fastapi import APIRouter

from src.api.app import storage

router = APIRouter()


@router.get("/files")
async def list_files(prefix: str = "") -> list[str]:
    """List keys under ``prefix`` in the default bucket."""
    return await storage.list_objects(prefix)
```

`list_objects` returns `[]` when nothing matches — aligned with the SDK convention ("no match is not an error").

### Batch delete

`remove_objects` deletes many keys with S3's `DeleteObjects` — one request
per 1000 keys instead of one `DELETE` per object — and returns only what the
store refused:

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AsyncMinIOClient

storage = AsyncMinIOClient(
    endpoint="localhost:9000",
    access_key="minioadmin",
    secret_key="minioadmin",
    default_bucket="uploads",
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Delete everything under a prefix."""
    keys = await storage.list_objects("tmp/")
    errors = await storage.remove_objects(keys)
    for error in errors:
        print(error.key, error.code, error.message)


asyncio.run(main())
```

An empty list is success. To delete **a data subject's files** (LGPD), use
`SubjectObjectStorage.delete_all` — see
[Data subject export and erasure](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/subject-data.md).

### Copy / move

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AsyncMinIOClient

from src.core.settings import settings

storage = AsyncMinIOClient(**settings.storage_kwargs())


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    await storage.copy_object("uploads/draft-1", "uploads/final-1")
    await storage.remove_object("uploads/draft-1")


asyncio.run(main())
```

## When NOT to use `AsyncMinIOClient`

- When you need operations **outside** the listed surface (SSE-KMS, S3 v2 ACLs, bucket replication). Use `storage.client.<method>` directly — `minio-py` stays accessible.
- For resumable uploads from the browser — `minio-py` does multipart automatically but does not resume an interrupted upload. Use the SDK's tus server: [Resumable uploads (tus)](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/resumable-upload.md), with `S3TusStore` over this same `AsyncMinIOClient`.

## Private bucket behind HTTPS

In production the guard refuses `STORAGE_SECURE=false` — with one
exception, for a common deployment shape: the S3-compatible server runs as
a container on the compose's private network (`STORAGE_ENDPOINT=bucket:9000`,
plain HTTP inside the network), and clients only ever see presigned URLs
for a public host whose TLS nginx terminates. Plain HTTP stays on the
private hop, and the guard accepts it when **all three** hold:

1. `STORAGE_ENDPOINT`'s host is private — a dot-less name (the Docker
   service name), `localhost`, a loopback, or an RFC 1918 IP (`10.x`,
   `172.16–31.x`, `192.168.x`), link-local or IPv6 ULA;
2. `STORAGE_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT` is set;
3. the public scheme is HTTPS — `STORAGE_PUBLIC_SECURE=true` (or a
   `STORAGE_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT` starting with `https://`).

Miss one and the violation stays, with a message naming the way out:

```text
- STORAGE_SECURE: storage traffic over plain HTTP (allowed only for a private STORAGE_ENDPOINT behind an HTTPS STORAGE_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT) [type=value_error]
```

The production `.env`:

```text
ENV=production
STORAGE_ENDPOINT=bucket:9000
STORAGE_SECURE=false
STORAGE_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT=storage.example.com
STORAGE_PUBLIC_SECURE=true
STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY=app-key
STORAGE_SECRET_KEY=app-secret-value
```

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    AsyncMinIOClient,
    BaseAppSettings,
    EnvironmentSettings,
    StorageSettings,
)


class Settings(EnvironmentSettings, StorageSettings, BaseAppSettings):
    """Bucket on the compose's private network, public URLs over HTTPS."""


settings = Settings()
print(settings.production_violations())
storage = AsyncMinIOClient(**settings.storage_kwargs())
print(storage.endpoint, storage.secure, storage.public_endpoint, storage.public_secure)
```

```text
[]
bucket:9000 False storage.example.com True
```

The app talks to `bucket:9000` over HTTP; presigned URLs are signed for
`storage.example.com` over HTTPS. The compose does not publish the
bucket's port — only nginx reaches it:

```yaml
services:
  bucket:
    image: mauriciobenjamin700/tempest-bucket:latest
    expose:
      - "9000"
  api:
    build: .
    env_file: .env
  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    ports:
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
      - ./certs:/etc/nginx/certs:ro
```

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name storage.example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/certs/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/certs/privkey.pem;

    location /minio/ {
        return 403;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://bucket:9000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https;
        client_max_body_size 100m;
    }
}
```

!!! warning "The `Host` must arrive untouched"
    SigV4 signs the `Host` header: the URL was signed for
    `storage.example.com`, so the bucket must receive that same `Host`.
    Hence `proxy_set_header Host $host` — without it nginx sends
    `bucket:9000` and every presigned URL answers `SignatureDoesNotMatch`.
    And do not expose the admin API: block the server's admin path
    (`/minio/` on MinIO and compatibles) and never publish the console
    port.

## One key per bucket

Some S3-compatible stores bind each access key to **one** bucket: the key
made for the public images can neither read nor write the private
documents. With a single credential, every upload, presigned URL, listing
and cleanup on the second bucket answers `AccessDenied`.

`STORAGE_BUCKET_CREDENTIALS` gives each bucket its own key. It is a JSON of
`bucket → {"access_key", "secret_key"}`; buckets missing from it keep
`STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY` / `STORAGE_SECRET_KEY`.

`.env`:

```bash
STORAGE_ENDPOINT=storage.example.com
STORAGE_SECURE=true
STORAGE_DEFAULT_BUCKET=images
STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY=images-key
STORAGE_SECRET_KEY=images-secret
STORAGE_BUCKET_CREDENTIALS='{"documents": {"access_key": "documents-key", "secret_key": "documents-secret"}}'
```

With it set, `build_storage_client()` returns a `BucketRoutedMinIOClient` —
a subclass of `AsyncMinIOClient`, so the service's annotation and calls do
not change. Every operation that takes `bucket` is signed with that
bucket's key, presigned URLs included:

```python
import asyncio
from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlsplit

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    BaseAppSettings,
    BucketRoutedMinIOClient,
    StorageSettings,
)


class Settings(StorageSettings, BaseAppSettings):
    """Two buckets, one key each."""


async def main() -> None:
    """Sign a link in each bucket and show which key signed it."""
    settings = Settings()
    print(settings.STORAGE_BUCKET_CREDENTIALS)
    storage = settings.build_storage_client()
    assert isinstance(storage, BucketRoutedMinIOClient)
    print(sorted(storage.routed_buckets))
    for bucket in ("images", "documents"):
        url = await storage.presigned_get_url("contract.pdf", bucket=bucket)
        credential = parse_qs(urlsplit(url).query)["X-Amz-Credential"][0]
        print(bucket, "->", credential.split("/")[0])


asyncio.run(main())
```

Signing is local (`minio` does not ask the server anything to sign once
`STORAGE_REGION` is set), so this runs with no bucket up:

```text
{'documents': StorageBucketCredential(access_key='documents-key', secret_key=SecretStr('**********'))}
['documents']
images -> images-key
documents -> documents-key
```

The secret is a `SecretStr`: masked in `repr`, `str` and `model_dump()`.

The routing rules:

- A **listed bucket** uses its key; a **bucket not listed** uses the
  primary one. A call without `bucket` goes to `STORAGE_DEFAULT_BUCKET`,
  routed like any other.
- **`list_buckets()` and the `client` attribute** name no bucket and stay
  on the primary credential.
- **`copy_object` with both buckets on the same credential** is the
  server's own copy, as before. **On different credentials** no key can
  read the source and write the destination at once, so the object is
  downloaded with the source key into a temporary file (deleted at the end)
  and uploaded with the destination key, carrying `Content-Type` and user
  metadata. The bytes cross the app on that path, and other stored headers
  (`Cache-Control`, `Content-Disposition`) are not copied.
- **`tempest storage`** builds the same client, so
  `tempest storage ls --bucket documents` signs with the documents key.

The boot refuses a half credential — a key without a secret, a secret
without a key, an empty value, or a misnamed field (`"secret"` instead of
`"secret_key"`) — and the error does not echo the value:

```text
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for Settings
STORAGE_BUCKET_CREDENTIALS.documents.secret_key
  Field required [type=missing]
```

Under `ENV=production` the guard also refuses a bucket whose secret is
still the local MinIO's `minioadmin`, and a non-empty
`STORAGE_BUCKET_CREDENTIALS` with `STORAGE_BACKEND=local`, which never
reads it.

!!! tip "Building the client by hand"
    `storage_kwargs()` does not change: `AsyncMinIOClient(**settings.storage_kwargs())`
    keeps a single credential. For routing, use
    `settings.build_storage_client()` or pass
    `bucket_credentials=settings.STORAGE_BUCKET_CREDENTIALS` to
    `BucketRoutedMinIOClient`.

## Storage switched off (`STORAGE_ENABLED=false`)

Going to production before the bucket exists? `STORAGE_ENABLED=false`
makes the production guard skip the `STORAGE_*` rules, and the same
`AsyncMinIOClient(**settings.storage_kwargs())` then refuses **every**
operation — the `client` attribute included — with
`IntegrationDisabledException` (`503`, `code="INTEGRATION_DISABLED"`,
`details={"integration": "storage"}`). A `SubjectObjectStorage` on top
inherits the refusal. No `if` in your code, and no `[minio]` extra needed
while the integration is off. The complete example is in
[Switching integrations on and off](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/system-checks.md#switching-integrations-on-and-off-phased-deploys).

## Recap

- `AsyncMinIOClient` is an async facade over the official `minio` package,
  behind the `[minio]` extra: buckets, objects and presigned URLs — what a
  FastAPI service usually needs.
- Configuration comes from the settings mixin, and the client is built in
  `create_app()`'s `lifespan` — one instance per process, not one per request.
- A presigned URL is how you hand over a private file without streaming the
  bytes through your own process.
- When the bytes must go through the backend, `download_response(key,
  request=request)` answers `206`, `304` and `416` — without the `request` it
  is always a full `200`.
- To have nginx deliver instead of the app, `serve_object` with
  `STORAGE_ACCEL_REDIRECT=true` answers `X-Accel-Redirect`; the internal
  `location` needs `proxy_pass` with a trailing slash, `Host` equal to
  `STORAGE_ENDPOINT` and the security `add_header` lines — nginx does not
  forward the app's.
- For the browser to open a private file through **the app's route**, sign
  the path in the mapper with `sign_path` and guard the route with
  `make_signed_path_dependency`: the signature covers path, `expires` and
  `purpose`, and a rejection is `403` (`SIGNED_URL_INVALID` or
  `SIGNED_URL_EXPIRED`).
- A store that binds each key to one bucket: `STORAGE_BUCKET_CREDENTIALS`
  makes `build_storage_client()` return the `BucketRoutedMinIOClient`, which
  signs each call with its bucket's key and falls back on the primary one.
- Anything outside the facade is not blocked: call `storage.client.<method>` and
  use `minio-py` directly, instead of waiting for the facade to grow.
- To switch between local disk and MinIO by configuration, the pluggable upload
  backend is the road — this facade is for a service that already chose MinIO.

## What's next

- The pluggable upload backend `MinIOUploadStorage` shipped in v0.24.0 — for the upload pipeline that switches between local disk and MinIO/S3 via a settings flag, see the [uploads recipe](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/uploads.md).


---

Source: https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/local-storage.md

# Storage on local disk — `LocalObjectStorageClient`

Your service keeps photos, exports and attachments, and until now that meant
an S3 server (MinIO, AWS, R2) running beside the API. For a service that runs
on one machine, that server is one more piece to start, upgrade and watch.

`LocalObjectStorageClient` keeps the objects **in a directory of the server
itself** and answers the same calls as
[`AsyncMinIOClient`](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/storage.md) — `put_object`, `stat_object`,
`stream_object`, `list_objects`, `remove_object`, `remove_objects`,
`presigned_get_url`, `presigned_put_url`. The rest of the service does not
change.

What changes is the link. A disk has no endpoint the browser can reach, so
the "presigned" link points at **your API**, signed with
[`sign_path`](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/reference/web-ui-utils/utils/#tempest_fastapi_sdk.utils.signed_url.sign_path),
and `make_local_storage_router` serves those routes.

No extra needed: only the standard library and the FastAPI the SDK already
brings. The optional encryption at rest needs `[storage-encryption]`.

## The first object

```python
import asyncio
from datetime import timedelta

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LocalObjectStorageClient


async def main() -> None:
    """Write, describe, read and sign an object on disk."""
    storage = LocalObjectStorageClient(
        "var/storage",
        public_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
        signing_secret="replace-with-a-long-secret",
    )
    etag = await storage.put_object(
        "reports/2026.txt",
        b"conteudo",
        content_type="text/plain",
    )
    stat = await storage.stat_object("reports/2026.txt")
    stream = await storage.stream_object("reports/2026.txt")
    body = b"".join([chunk async for chunk in stream])
    link = await storage.presigned_get_url(
        "reports/2026.txt", expires=timedelta(minutes=10)
    )
    print(etag, stat.size, stat.content_type, body)
    print(link)


asyncio.run(main())
```

Running it prints something like:

```text
b59853db2f3ef8f156a72e38c30ba7d2 8 text/plain b'conteudo'
http://127.0.0.1:8000/storage/uploads/reports/2026.txt?expires=1792869637&signature=tvsYmCeLaH3y...
```

Piece by piece:

* `"var/storage"` is the root. The client creates `objects/`, `meta/` and
  `tmp/` inside it.
* The default bucket is `"uploads"` (`default_bucket=`). Each bucket is a
  subfolder of `objects/`.
* `put_object` returns the ETag, the MD5 of the bytes, as S3 answers for a
  single-part upload.
* `stat_object` reads size and date from the file, and content type and
  metadata from the metadata file stored beside it.
* The link lasts 10 minutes and only opens that object's route.

!!! info "What it looks like on disk"
    ```text
    var/storage/
      objects/uploads/reports/2026.txt          the bytes
      meta/uploads/reports/2026.txt.meta.json   content type, metadata, ETag
      tmp/                                      writes in flight
    ```
    Every write goes to `tmp/` first and is moved into place with
    `os.replace`. A reader sees the old object or the new one, never half of
    one.

## Serving the links from the API

The link points at `<public_url><route_prefix>/<bucket>/<key>`. Mount the
router **at the app root**, with no extra `prefix`: the signature covers the
path the app sees, and the router already carries the client's
`route_prefix`.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    LocalObjectStorageClient,
    make_local_storage_router,
    register_exception_handlers,
)

storage = LocalObjectStorageClient(
    "var/storage",
    public_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
    signing_secret="replace-with-a-long-secret",
    route_prefix="/api/storage",
    max_upload_bytes=5 * 1024 * 1024,
)

app = FastAPI()
register_exception_handlers(app)
app.include_router(make_local_storage_router(storage))


@app.get("/api/photos/{name}")
async def photo_link(name: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Return a 15-minute link to the photo (authorize first)."""
    return {"url": await storage.presigned_get_url(f"photos/{name}")}


@app.post("/api/photos/{name}/upload-url")
async def upload_link(name: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Return a direct upload link for the photo."""
    return {"url": await storage.presigned_put_url(f"photos/{name}")}
```

The two routes the router mounts:

| Route | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/storage/{bucket}/{key}` | checks the download signature and serves the file with its stored content type, with `Range` (`206`), `If-None-Match` (`304`) and `416` |
| `PUT /api/storage/{bucket}/{key}` | checks the upload signature and stores the raw body with the request's `Content-Type`; answers `200` with the `ETag` |

The app's client uploads like this, with no token: the link is the
credential.

```bash
curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: image/jpeg" --data-binary @photo.jpg "<upload url>"
```

!!! tip "Download and upload do not mix"
    `GET` and `PUT` links are signed for different purposes. A download link
    used in a `PUT` answers `403 SIGNED_URL_INVALID` and stores nothing, and
    the other way round too.

The router's error responses:

| Situation | Response |
| --- | --- |
| no signature, tampered signature, or another purpose | `403 SIGNED_URL_INVALID` |
| expired link | `403 SIGNED_URL_EXPIRED` |
| object that does not exist (download) | `404 NOT_FOUND` |
| body over `max_upload_bytes` | `413 FILE_TOO_LARGE`, leaving no file |

The cap holds even without `Content-Length`: the body is counted as it
arrives and cut when it passes the limit.

!!! warning "The payload is not signed"
    As with S3, the upload link only fixes **where** the file goes, not what
    it is. Check size and type with `stat_object` (and the first bytes with
    `stream_object`) before trusting the object.

## Capped upload and download with a signed type

The two S3 features the plain `PUT` and `GET` lack exist here under the same
call, so the service switches backend without touching the app's client.

`presigned_post_policy` returns a `PresignedPost` (URL + form fields). The
`POST /api/storage/{bucket}/{key}` route reads the `multipart/form-data` and
applies the signed limits before storing:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    LocalObjectStorageClient,
    make_local_storage_router,
    register_exception_handlers,
)

storage = LocalObjectStorageClient(
    "var/storage",
    public_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
    signing_secret="replace-with-a-long-secret",
    route_prefix="/api/storage",
    max_upload_bytes=5 * 1024 * 1024,
)

app = FastAPI()
register_exception_handlers(app)
app.include_router(make_local_storage_router(storage))


@app.post("/api/photos/{name}/form")
async def upload_form(name: str) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Form that accepts only JPEG up to 2 MiB."""
    post = await storage.presigned_post_policy(
        f"photos/{name}",
        max_bytes=2 * 1024 * 1024,
        content_type="image/jpeg",
    )
    return {"url": post.url, "fields": post.fields}


@app.get("/api/photos/{name}/inline")
async def inline_link(name: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Link that opens the photo inline, as JPEG."""
    url = await storage.presigned_get_url(
        f"photos/{name}",
        media_type="image/jpeg",
        as_attachment=False,
    )
    return {"url": url}
```

| `POST` case | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| file within `[min_bytes, max_bytes]` | `204`, with the `ETag` |
| over `max_bytes` | `413 FILE_TOO_LARGE`, nothing stored |
| under `min_bytes` | `400 FILE_TOO_SMALL`, nothing stored |
| `Content-Type` or `key` field other than the signed one | `403 SIGNED_URL_INVALID` |
| `max_bytes` (or another limit) edited in the URL | `403 SIGNED_URL_INVALID` |

The limits and the `GET` overrides travel in the query, and the SDK binds
them to the signature (`bound_purpose`): changing one verifies as another
purpose and fails. A link signed with none of them still works as before.

!!! note "Needs the `[upload]` extra"
    Reading the form takes `python-multipart`. The check runs in
    `presigned_post_policy`, so a missing extra breaks where the link is
    issued, not on the user's upload.

!!! info "`max_bytes` up to `max_upload_bytes`"
    The form's cap cannot exceed the store's: asking for more raises
    `ValueError` when signing.

## Picking the backend from settings

`StorageSettings` picks between S3 and disk with `STORAGE_BACKEND`, and
`build_storage_client()` builds the right client:

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    AsyncMinIOClient,
    BaseAppSettings,
    LocalObjectStorageClient,
    StorageSettings,
)


class Settings(StorageSettings, BaseAppSettings):
    """The service's settings."""


settings = Settings()
client: AsyncMinIOClient | LocalObjectStorageClient = settings.build_storage_client()
```

```env
STORAGE_BACKEND=local
STORAGE_LOCAL_DIR=/var/lib/app/storage
STORAGE_LOCAL_PUBLIC_URL=https://api.example.com
STORAGE_LOCAL_ROUTE_PREFIX=/api/storage
STORAGE_LOCAL_SIGNING_SECRET=a-long-random-secret
STORAGE_LOCAL_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES=5242880
STORAGE_DEFAULT_BUCKET=media
```

| Variable | Default | What for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `STORAGE_BACKEND` | `s3` | `local` turns the disk on |
| `STORAGE_LOCAL_DIR` | `var/storage` | the store's root |
| `STORAGE_LOCAL_PUBLIC_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:8000` | start of the links |
| `STORAGE_LOCAL_ROUTE_PREFIX` | `/storage` | path of the routes, as the app sees it |
| `STORAGE_LOCAL_SIGNING_SECRET` | dev placeholder | secret of the links |
| `STORAGE_LOCAL_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | 25 MiB | `PUT` cap |

With `ENV=production` (`EnvironmentSettings`) and `STORAGE_BACKEND=local`, the
boot refuses the development secret, a `STORAGE_LOCAL_PUBLIC_URL` without
`https` and a relative `STORAGE_LOCAL_DIR`. The S3 credentials are no longer
checked, because nothing reads them.

!!! tip "Reusing `JWT_SECRET`"
    The signature derives its key from the secret **and** the purpose, so
    putting the `JWT_SECRET` value in `STORAGE_LOCAL_SIGNING_SECRET` is safe:
    a link never works as a token, and the other way round.

## With `SubjectObjectStorage`

The local client satisfies `SubjectStorageClient`, so per-subject export and
erasure (LGPD) work the same:

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LocalObjectStorageClient
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.privacy import SubjectObjectStorage


async def main() -> None:
    """Store two files of a subject and erase them all at once."""
    client = LocalObjectStorageClient(
        "var/storage",
        public_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
        signing_secret="replace-with-a-long-secret",
    )
    storage = SubjectObjectStorage(client, prefix="users")
    await storage.put(42, "avatar.png", b"png", content_type="image/png")
    await storage.put(42, "export.json", b"{}", content_type="application/json")
    print(await storage.names(42))
    print(await storage.delete_all(42))


asyncio.run(main())
```

```text
['avatar.png', 'export.json']
2
```

A missing object raises `LocalObjectNotFoundError`, a `FileNotFoundError`
with `code = "NoSuchKey"` — the code S3 answers. Code that branches on the S3
error's `code` keeps working.

## Encryption at rest

So far the files sit **in plaintext** on the disk. If your service keeps a
photo of an ID, of a notebook or anything personal, whoever reaches the disk,
a snapshot of the volume or a backup of it reads everything — even when the
database encrypts its content columns.

The bytes come in and go out through paths the SDK owns (the signed
`PUT`/`POST` the app calls directly, the signed `GET`, `download_response`),
so the encryption lives in the client: pass `encryption_keys` and every write
path encrypts, every read path decrypts. The rest of the service does not
change.

### Generating the key

Each key is 32 bytes (AES-256). Generate one in base64:

```bash
python -c "import os,base64;print(base64.b64encode(os.urandom(32)).decode())"
```

```text
2yk6fNE3HpXOhHypqJSA3ncp6UWjTI/4jORNYXz2RDo=
```

And install the extra that brings the cipher (`cryptography`):

```bash
uv add "tempest-fastapi-sdk[storage-encryption]"
```

### The first encrypted object

```python
import asyncio
import os

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LocalObjectStorageClient


async def main() -> None:
    """Store an encrypted object, look at the disk and read it back."""
    storage = LocalObjectStorageClient(
        "var/storage",
        public_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
        signing_secret="change-me-to-a-long-secret",
        encryption_keys={"2026-11": os.urandom(32)},
    )
    await storage.put_object(
        "notebooks/photo.jpg",
        b"notebook contents",
        content_type="image/jpeg",
    )
    on_disk = storage.object_path("notebooks/photo.jpg").read_bytes()
    stat = await storage.stat_object("notebooks/photo.jpg")
    stream = await storage.stream_object("notebooks/photo.jpg")
    body = b"".join([chunk async for chunk in stream])
    print(on_disk[:8], b"notebook" in on_disk, len(on_disk))
    print(stat.size, body)


asyncio.run(main())
```

```text
b'TFSDKENC' False 57
17 b'notebook contents'
```

Piece by piece:

* `encryption_keys` is a dictionary of **id → key**. The id is written in
  every file's header; the key, never.
* The file on disk starts with the `TFSDKENC` marker and does not hold the
  text: 57 bytes for 17 of content (header + a 16-byte tag per block).
* `stat_object` answers the **plaintext** size (17), which is what you compare
  against an upload cap.
* `stream_object` returns the original bytes.

!!! warning "The example's key dies with the process"
    `os.urandom(32)` in code is there to watch the cipher work. In a service
    the key comes from the environment (see the settings below): without it,
    nothing that was written opens again.

### How it works

The file is cut into 64 KiB blocks (`LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_BLOCK_SIZE`) and each
block is sealed with AES-256-GCM, from `cryptography`. It is the STREAM
construction:

* each block's nonce is a random per-file prefix + the block number + a
  "last block" flag;
* the header (format version, key id, prefix) and the object's
  `<bucket>/<key>` are authenticated data.

So writes and reads keep streaming, without loading the whole file, and every
tampering turns into an error:

| What happened to the file | Result |
| --- | --- |
| a byte changed in the content, a tag or the nonce prefix | `StorageIntegrityException`, `reason="authentication"` |
| unknown version or header cut short | `reason="format"` |
| blocks out of order | `reason="authentication"` |
| last block removed | `reason="authentication"` |
| cut inside a tag | `reason="format"` |
| copied or renamed to another key or bucket | `reason="authentication"` |
| sealed with a key the client does not hold | `reason="unknown_key"` |
| a plaintext file, without `allow_plaintext_read` | `reason="plaintext"` |

`StorageIntegrityException` is an `AppException` with status `500` and
`code="STORAGE_INTEGRITY_ERROR"`. Its `details` carry the `reason` only —
never the object's name or any byte of it.

!!! check "No unauthenticated byte"
    Each block is handed out only after its tag verified. The first block is
    checked **before** `stream_object` returns the stream, so through the
    router a tampered file answers a clean `500 STORAGE_INTEGRITY_ERROR`. If
    a block in the middle fails, the response has already started: the
    connection is cut after the blocks that verified (measured with uvicorn
    and httpx: `200`, two 64 KiB blocks received, then `RemoteProtocolError`
    for the missing rest of the `Content-Length`).

### Through the API, nothing changes

`make_local_storage_router` keeps its shape:

* the signed `PUT` and `POST` store encrypted; the cap (`max_upload_bytes`,
  `max_bytes`) counts the content, not the header and the tags;
* the signed `GET` serves plaintext, with the content's `Content-Length`;
* `Range` works: the client decrypts only the blocks the range covers.
  `SubjectObjectStorage.read(..., max_bytes=...)` also stops at the limit and
  decrypts nothing past it.

### From settings

```env
STORAGE_BACKEND=local
STORAGE_LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_KEYS='{"2026-11":"2yk6fNE3HpXOhHypqJSA3ncp6UWjTI/4jORNYXz2RDo="}'
```

| Variable | Default | What for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `STORAGE_LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` | `{}` | JSON of id → base64 key; the **first** writes, all read |
| `STORAGE_LOCAL_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_READ` | `false` | reads an old file without a header as plaintext (during the migration only) |

`local_storage_kwargs()` decodes the keys and passes `encryption_keys` and
`allow_plaintext_read` to the client, so `build_storage_client()` comes out
encrypting. Without keys the dictionary is the one it always was. A key that
is not the base64 of 32 bytes fails the boot with its id in the message,
never its value.

!!! info "Production without a key: a warning, not a refusal"
    With `ENV=production`, `STORAGE_BACKEND=local` and no key, the boot
    **goes on** and logs a `WARNING` on the `tempest_fastapi_sdk.settings`
    logger. Refusing would break, without notice, every service that already
    runs the local backend in production on the day it upgrades. Switch the
    encryption on and the warning goes away.

### Migrating a volume that already has files

A file written before the key has no header. With the key on it is refused
(`reason="plaintext"`), unless you allow plaintext reads during the
migration:

1. Generate the key and deploy with both variables:

    ```env
    STORAGE_LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_KEYS='{"2026-11":"<base64>"}'
    STORAGE_LOCAL_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_READ=true
    ```

    From here on, every new file is written encrypted, and the old ones keep
    opening.

2. Encrypt what exists, ideally in a window without writes:

    !!! info "The `tempest` command needs the `[cli]` extra (or `[cli-ops]` on a server)"
        Without either, `tempest` exits with code 2 and prints how to install it.
        In development: `uv add --dev "tempest-fastapi-sdk[cli]"`. Details in
        [Installation → CLI](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/installation.md#cli).

    ```bash
    tempest storage encrypt-local
    ```

    ```text
    docs: 1 object(s) encrypted
    uploads: 1 object(s) encrypted
    ```

    The command walks every bucket of `STORAGE_LOCAL_DIR` (`--bucket` limits
    it to one) and is **idempotent**: an encrypted file is skipped, so running
    it again after an interruption rewrites nothing. Content type and
    metadata stay; the ETag becomes the MD5 of the encrypted file.

3. Remove `STORAGE_LOCAL_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_READ` and restart.

In code the same is `await storage.encrypt_existing()` (per bucket, with
`await storage.list_buckets()`).

!!! warning "Writes during the migration"
    Each file is rewritten in `tmp/` and only swapped in if it did not change
    while it was read (same inode, size and time). The check and the swap are
    two steps, so a write landing exactly between them is lost. Run it with
    the service stopped or with no upload in flight.

### Rotating the key

The first key of the JSON writes; any key reads, by the header's id:

1. Put the new key **first** and keep the old one:

    ```env
    STORAGE_LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_KEYS='{"2027-05":"<new>","2026-11":"<old>"}'
    ```

    New writes go out under `2027-05`; what is under `2026-11` keeps
    opening.

2. Rewrite what is under the old key:

    ```bash
    tempest storage reencrypt-local
    ```

    Idempotent too: what is already under the first key is skipped. A file
    that does not decrypt (its key left the ring, the file is damaged) stops
    the command with the error and exit code `1`, rewriting nothing of it. In
    code: `await storage.reencrypt()`.

3. Remove the old key from the JSON.

### What the encryption protects, and what it does not

It protects the files **at rest**: the disk, a snapshot of the volume, a
backup copied elsewhere, a volume mounted by mistake on another machine.

It does not protect:

* **a compromised process.** The API decrypts to serve; whoever runs code in
  it reads what it reads.
* **the key next to the data.** A key in the `.env` that travels with the
  volume in the same backup is a padlock with the key hanging from it. Keep
  it in a secrets manager, or at least out of the volume and its backup.
* **what leaked before the migration.** Old backups and snapshots stay in
  plaintext, and the disk may keep the freed blocks of the old file. Rotate
  the old backups out of retention.
* **the metadata.** The key name (`<bucket>/<key>`), content type, user
  metadata and the approximate size stay visible on disk.

!!! tip "One key per environment"
    Development, staging and production with different keys: a production
    backup restored by mistake elsewhere does not open.

## Before going to production

!!! warning "One machine only"
    The disk belongs to **one** server. Two API instances on different
    machines do not see each other's files. Once you scale past one machine,
    go back to S3 (`STORAGE_BACKEND=s3`).

!!! warning "API and worker on the same volume"
    Processes on the same machine share the store by mounting **the same
    directory**. In `docker compose`, that is a named volume mounted at the
    same path in the API and in the worker:

    ```yaml
    services:
      api:
        volumes:
          - storage:/var/lib/app/storage
      worker:
        volumes:
          - storage:/var/lib/app/storage

    volumes:
      storage:
    ```

!!! warning "Backup is yours"
    Managed S3 replicates the data; a directory does not. Add
    `STORAGE_LOCAL_DIR` (with `objects/` and `meta/`) to the server's backup
    routine.

??? info "Technical details"
    * Every blocking call runs in `asyncio.to_thread`.
    * An empty key, one starting with `/`, with a `.` or `..` segment, with
      `\` or NUL, or with a segment ending in `.meta.json` is refused with
      `ValueError`. The final path is resolved (following symlinks) and must
      stay under the root.
    * On a disk, keys `a` and `a/b` cannot coexist (`a` cannot be a file and a
      folder at once); writing the second raises `OSError`
      (`FileExistsError` or `IsADirectoryError`, depending on the order). S3
      accepts both.
    * `list_objects(recursive=False)` returns "folders" ending in `/`, as S3
      does. A prefix whose directory part has an empty, `.` or `..` segment,
      or that resolves outside the bucket (a symlink included), returns `[]`
      — on S3 `../` is just characters no key starts with.
    * `remove_objects` returns `AccessDenied` for a permission error and
      `InternalError` for anything else, one `ObjectDeleteError` per key.
    * `X-Accel-Redirect` is not supported by the local client: `GET` always
      goes through the API.

## Recap

* `LocalObjectStorageClient` keeps objects in a directory and speaks the same
  language as `AsyncMinIOClient`.
* The "presigned" links point at the API; `make_local_storage_router` serves
  them, at the app root.
* `STORAGE_BACKEND=local` + `build_storage_client()` swap the backend without
  touching the rest of the service.
* One machine only, a volume shared by the API and the worker, a backup of
  the directory.
* `encryption_keys` (`STORAGE_LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_KEYS`) seals each file in
  AES-256-GCM blocks: the first key writes, all read, and tampering turns into
  `StorageIntegrityException`.
* `tempest storage encrypt-local` migrates an old volume and
  `tempest storage reencrypt-local` closes a rotation; both are idempotent.
* The encryption protects the disk, snapshots and backups; it does not protect
  the process or a key kept next to the data.


---

Source: https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/stripe.md

# Stripe (cards, subscriptions, Checkout)

Every service of ours that charges a card used to rewrite the same Stripe
layer: a synchronous HTTP client called from inside an async route,
hand-retyped schemas, and a webhook verification each one derived its own
way. `tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe` ships that layer.

!!! info "Installation"
    No extra. The integration uses the `HTTPClient` the SDK already has,
    and `httpx` ships in the base package. The `[http]` extra exists and is
    optional: it only declares `httpx` explicitly.

!!! info "When to use this"
    International card payments, subscriptions or hosted Checkout. For
    **Pix**, use [OpenPix](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/openpix.md), which is generated from the
    provider's specification.

## The minimal path

```python
import asyncio
from decimal import Decimal

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    StripeClient,
    stripe_http_client,
    to_minor_units,
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    client = StripeClient(stripe_http_client("sk_test_..."))
    intent = await client.payment_intents.create(
        {
            "amount": to_minor_units(Decimal("199.90"), "brl"),
            "currency": "brl",
            "automatic_payment_methods": {"enabled": True},
            "metadata": {"order_id": "1042"},
        }
    )
    print(intent.id, intent.status, intent.client_secret)


asyncio.run(main())
```

Three things happened without being asked for: the body went out
**form-encoded** in bracket notation (`metadata[order_id]=1042`), the
request carried an `Idempotency-Key`, and the `Stripe-Version` header
pinned the API version.

!!! danger "`client_secret` is a credential"
    It authorizes confirming **that** payment. It belongs in the response
    to the order's own owner and nowhere else — never in a log, never in
    telemetry.

## How it works, piece by piece

### The body is form-encoded, not JSON

Stripe **accepts no JSON** on writes: all 588 write operations in the
specification declare `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. Nesting is
brackets:

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import form_encode

print(
    form_encode(
        {
            "mode": "payment",
            "line_items": [{"price": "price_123", "quantity": 2}],
            "metadata": {"order_id": "1042"},
        }
    )
)
```

```text
{'mode': 'payment',
 'line_items[0][price]': 'price_123',
 'line_items[0][quantity]': '2',
 'metadata[order_id]': '1042'}
```

`form_encode` is public and serves any form-encoded API — and **the SDK's
integration generator now uses the same function**: an operation whose
`requestBody` declares form comes out with `data=form_encode(payload)`
instead of `json=payload`. Before that, a client generated against Stripe
had 100% of its writes rejected.

What `form_encode` decides for you:

| Value | Goes as | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `True` / `False` | `true` / `false` | `str(True)` would send `"True"` |
| `None` | **not sent** | an empty string is a real value — it *clears* the field |
| `Decimal("10.50")` | `10.50` | going through `float` loses a cent |
| `Enum` | its `.value` | `str()` would send `"Class.MEMBER"` |
| `datetime` | ISO-8601 | |

### Money: zero-decimal currencies exist

Stripe charges in the **smallest unit**. For most currencies that is a
cent, but for JPY, KRW, VND and 13 others the smallest unit **is** the
unit — and dividing everything by 100 is a silent billing bug no BRL-only
test will catch.

```python
from decimal import Decimal

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    from_minor_units,
    to_minor_units,
)

print(to_minor_units(Decimal("10.50"), "brl"))    # 1050
print(to_minor_units(Decimal("1050"), "jpy"))     # 1050  <- not 105000
print(from_minor_units(1050, "jpy"))              # Decimal('1050')
print(to_minor_units(Decimal("10.505"), "bhd"))   # 10505 (three decimals)
```

Both tables (`ZERO_DECIMAL_CURRENCIES`, `THREE_DECIMAL_CURRENCIES`) come
from Stripe's documentation and are pinned by a test, so an upstream
change shows up as a failure here — not as a hundredfold charge.

### Webhooks: what Stripe signs is not the body

The header is `t=<timestamp>,v1=<hmac>`, and the HMAC covers
`f"{t}.{body}"`. Signing the body alone is the most common mistake in a
hand-rolled verification — and it fails *silently*, as a 401 on every
delivery.

```python
from typing import Any

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    StripeEvent,
    StripeWebhookEvent,
    make_stripe_webhook_dependency,
)

from src.core.settings import settings

router = APIRouter(prefix="/webhooks", tags=["webhooks"])
verified = make_stripe_webhook_dependency(settings.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET)


@router.post("/stripe", include_in_schema=False)
async def stripe_webhook(
    event: StripeWebhookEvent = Depends(verified),
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Receive an already verified, typed delivery."""
    if event.event is StripeEvent.PAYMENT_INTENT_SUCCEEDED:
        return {"handled": True, "intent": event.data_object["id"]}
    return {"handled": False, "type": event.event_type}
```

- An invalid, missing or out-of-window (5 minutes) signature is a **401**
  before your handler runs.
- An empty (or blank) secret **fails the boot**:
  `make_stripe_webhook_dependency("")` raises `ValueError` while the router
  is built, and `verify_signature(..., "")` returns `False`. An HMAC under
  an empty key is computable by anyone, so a `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`
  missing from the environment never becomes an endpoint that accepts
  forged deliveries.
- Secret rotation works: Stripe sends one `v1` per active secret and any
  match is accepted.
- An unknown event type does **not** take the route down — `event` is
  `None` and `event_type` keeps the string. A Stripe release does not
  become your incident.
- `event_id` is there to **deduplicate**: deliveries repeat by design.

!!! warning "A verified signature is not authorization"
    It proves the delivery came from Stripe. It does not prove the state
    you are about to change is current — deliveries repeat and arrive out
    of order. Before releasing goods on `payment_intent.succeeded`,
    re-read the intent through the API.

So a test never re-derives the signature wrongly, the module exports the
signer:

```python
import json

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import sign_payload

body = json.dumps({"id": "evt_1", "type": "payment_intent.succeeded"}).encode()
header = sign_payload(body, "whsec_test", timestamp=1_770_000_000)
```

### The 265 event types, as an enum

`StripeEvent` is **generated** from the specification — from the
`enabled_events` parameter of `POST /v1/webhook_endpoints`, which is
where Stripe enumerates the types (the `event` object does not). A drift
test fails if the file is edited by hand.

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import StripeEvent

print(StripeEvent.INVOICE_PAID.value)               # invoice.paid
print(StripeEvent.has_value("customer.created"))    # True
```

### Idempotency: why every write carries a key

A timeout on `POST /v1/payment_intents` leaves you not knowing whether
money moved. A retry without a key creates a second payment; with one,
Stripe replays the original response for 24 hours. The client puts a
UUID4 on every write — swap in your own when you want the window to cover
your flow:

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    StripeClient,
    stripe_http_client,
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    client = StripeClient(stripe_http_client("sk_test_..."))
    order_id = "1042"
    await client.payment_intents.create(
        {"amount": 19990, "currency": "brl"},
        idempotency_key=f"order-{order_id}",
    )


asyncio.run(main())
```

### Cursor pagination

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    StripeClient,
    stripe_http_client,
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    client = StripeClient(stripe_http_client("sk_test_..."))
    filters = {"created": {"gte": 1_770_000_000}}
    async for customer in client.customers.auto_paginate(filters):
        print(customer.id, customer.email)


asyncio.run(main())
```

The cursor is the **last item's id**, not an offset, so the walk stays
correct while objects are created underneath it.

### Errors that say what happened

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    StripeClient,
    StripeError,
    stripe_http_client,
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    client = StripeClient(stripe_http_client("sk_test_..."))
    try:
        await client.payment_intents.create({"amount": 19990, "currency": "brl"})
    except StripeError as error:
        print(error.status_code)    # 402
        print(error.error_type)     # card_error
        print(error.code)           # card_declined
        print(error.decline_code)   # insufficient_funds
        print(error.request_id)     # req_... (what Stripe support asks for)


asyncio.run(main())
```

The id that `retrieve`, `update` and `delete` take becomes **one** path
segment: `/`, `?` and `#` are encoded (`quote(..., safe="")`), and `""`,
`"."` and `".."` raise `ValueError` before sending. Up to v0.334.1 the id
went in raw, and an id holding `/`, `..` or `?` addressed another Stripe
resource, with the same secret key and the same method.

The response is checked too. Every Stripe object names its own type in the
`object` field (`"customer"`, `"payment_intent"`, `"checkout.session"`), and
a `delete` tombstone keeps the deleted object's type. `create`, `retrieve`,
`update` and `delete` on the `StripeClient` resources raise
`StripeObjectMismatchError` when a `2xx` carries another type or none —
instead of validating another family's object into the wrong model:

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    StripeClient,
    StripeObjectMismatchError,
    stripe_http_client,
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    client = StripeClient(stripe_http_client("sk_test_..."))
    try:
        await client.customers.retrieve("cus_123")
    except StripeObjectMismatchError as error:
        print(error.expected_object)   # customer
        print(error.received_object)   # the type that came back ("" without the field)
        print(error.status_code)       # the response's 2xx


asyncio.run(main())
```

It subclasses `StripeError`, so an existing `except StripeError` keeps
catching it. Behaviour change: up to v0.335.0 the body was returned
unchecked. A `StripeResource` you build by hand only checks when given
`object_type=`.

### Thin models, nothing lost

The models name the fields that carry decisions — `status`, `amount`,
`currency`, the ids linking objects — and set `extra="allow"`. The rest
of the object stays reachable:

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    StripeClient,
    stripe_http_client,
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    client = StripeClient(stripe_http_client("sk_test_..."))
    intent = await client.payment_intents.retrieve("pi_123")
    print(intent.status)                                  # typed
    print((intent.model_extra or {}).get("next_action"))  # preserved


asyncio.run(main())
```

An expandable field (`customer`, `payment_intent`, …) is a `str`: without
`expand`, Stripe sends the id. Ask for the object and read it from
`model_extra`:

```python
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    StripeClient,
    stripe_http_client,
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    client = StripeClient(stripe_http_client("sk_test_..."))
    intent = await client.payment_intents.retrieve(
        "pi_123", params={"expand": ["customer"]}
    )
    print(intent.customer)


asyncio.run(main())
```

!!! note "Why this client is hand-written rather than generated"
    The SDK generates integrations from OpenAPI — OpenPix is generated.
    Stripe's specification does not survive the trip, and that was
    **measured** on `2026-07-29.dahlia`:

    - generating the full surface yields a `schemas.py` of **3.3 MB / 81k
      lines**, and importing it costs **5.8 s and 492 MB of RSS**;
    - slicing by resource does not help: `/v1/prices` **alone** reaches
      864 of the 1440 schemas, and the ten core resources together reach
      1020. There is no small subset.

    So what comes from the specification still comes from it — API
    version, base URL and the 265 events, via `make stripe-fetch` — and
    the rest is code that fits in your head. The numbers, and how to
    reproduce them, are in `scripts/regen_stripe.py`.

## Configuration

```python
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import BaseAppSettings
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    StripeClient,
    stripe_http_client,
)


class Settings(BaseAppSettings):
    """Service settings."""

    STRIPE_API_KEY: str = ""
    STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET: str = ""


settings = Settings()
client = StripeClient(stripe_http_client(settings.STRIPE_API_KEY))
```

The webhook secret is **per endpoint**, not per account: a service with a
test and a live endpoint has two. The example's `""` default only lets
`Settings` load in tests: with it, building the webhook router raises
`ValueError`.

## Testing

Inject an `httpx.MockTransport` and inspect the request that would go
out:

```python
from urllib.parse import parse_qs

import httpx

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.integrations.payment.stripe import (
    StripeClient,
    stripe_http_client,
)

requests: list[httpx.Request] = []


def handler(request: httpx.Request) -> httpx.Response:
    """Record the request and answer with a fake customer."""
    requests.append(request)
    return httpx.Response(200, json={"id": "cus_1", "object": "customer"})


async def test_create_customer() -> None:
    """The write goes out form-encoded, in bracket notation."""
    client = StripeClient(
        stripe_http_client("sk_test_x", transport=httpx.MockTransport(handler))
    )

    await client.customers.create({"email": "ana@example.com", "metadata": {"o": "1"}})

    assert parse_qs(requests[-1].content.decode()) == {
        "email": ["ana@example.com"],
        "metadata[o]": ["1"],
    }
```

## Recap

- `StripeClient` over the SDK's `HTTPClient`: retry, circuit breaker and
  the pinned `Stripe-Version` come from one place.
- Writes are form-encoded in bracket notation (`form_encode`, public and
  now used by the generator too) and carry an `Idempotency-Key` by
  default.
- Money respects zero-decimal and three-decimal currencies.
- Webhooks verify over `t.body`, with a replay window, secret rotation,
  and an unknown event type that does not take the route down.
- 265 events as an enum, generated from the specification with a drift
  test.
- Thin models with `extra="allow"` — the client is hand-written because
  generating the whole specification costs 3.3 MB and 492 MB of RSS,
  measured.


---

Source: https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/recipes/system-checks.md

# System checks (`tempest check-config`)

Validate configuration **before** serving traffic — empty signing
secret, CORS `*` with credentials, SQLite in production. A Django-style
check framework: functions inspect your settings and emit messages; the
CLI (or a startup hook) runs them all and fails if any is serious.

## The problem

A deploy with an empty `JWT_SECRET` boots happily and only breaks (or
worse, accepts forged tokens) in production. Config errors don't show up
in tests — they depend on the environment. There was no place to declare
"this must be true to ship".

## Running the built-in checks

The SDK ships checks for the most common slips. Run them against your
settings:

!!! info "The `tempest` command needs the `[cli]` extra (or `[cli-ops]` on a server)"
    Without either, `tempest` exits with code 2 and prints how to install it.
    In development: `uv add --dev "tempest-fastapi-sdk[cli]"`. Details in
    [Installation → CLI](https://mauriciobenjamin700.github.io/tempest-fastapi-sdk/en/installation.md#cli).

```bash
tempest check-config
```

The CLI auto-detects the settings object at conventional locations
(`src.core.settings:settings`, `app.core.settings:settings`, …). Point it
explicitly when needed:

```bash
tempest check-config --settings src.core.settings:settings
```

Typical output:

```text
WARNING: (security.W004) JWT_SECRET still holds the default declared by its settings field — a deployment that never set it signs tokens with a value that lives in source control.
	HINT: Generate one with `tempest secrets rotate`.
INFO: (deployment.I001) SERVER_DEBUG is enabled.
	HINT: Ensure SERVER_DEBUG is off in production (it leaks internals).
2 message(s), 0 at/above ERROR.
```

It exits **non-zero** when any message reaches `--fail-level` (default
`error`) — so it doubles as a CI gate and a pre-deploy check. Raise the
bar to treat warnings as blocking:

```bash
tempest check-config --fail-level warning
```

Built-in checks (all best-effort — they skip silently when the attribute
is absent from your settings):

| id | Level | What |
|----|-------|------|
| `security.W001` / `W002` | WARNING | `JWT_SECRET` / `SECRET_KEY` / `TOKEN_SECRET` empty or < 32 chars |
| `security.W003` | WARNING | CORS `*` **with** credentials |
| `security.W004` | WARNING | secret still equal to the default declared on its own field |
| `database.W001` | WARNING | SQLite `DATABASE_URL` with debug off |
| `deployment.I001` | INFO | `SERVER_DEBUG` (or `DEBUG`) on |
| `deployment.I002` | INFO | bind on `0.0.0.0` |

!!! warning "The secret that passed was the only one guaranteed to be wrong"
    Up to v0.271.0, `security.W002` only rejected a secret shorter than
    32 characters — and the placeholder the SDK itself ships in
    `JWTSettings.JWT_SECRET` is **exactly** 32. A deployment that forgot
    to set `JWT_SECRET` signed tokens with a value published in the SDK
    source, and `tempest check-config` reported everything as fine.

    `security.W004` compares the value against
    `model_fields[name].default`, never against a copy of the string —
    so it keeps holding the day the placeholder changes.

!!! note "Which field the debug check reads"
    `deployment.I001` and `database.W001` resolve debug by name
    precedence: `SERVER_DEBUG` first (the name the `ServerSettings`
    mixin declares), then `DEBUG`, so a project that declared one by
    hand keeps working. Up to v0.271.0 both read only `DEBUG` — `I001`
    never fired, and `database.W001` warned backwards, complaining
    about SQLite precisely when debug was **on**.

## Writing your own check
